data.title: TradingView MCP: When Artificial Intelligence Got Its Hands On The Pine Script Compiler
data.description:
A few years ago, developing a trading strategy began with learning a programming language. Then came large language models, and traders could describe their ideas in plain English. There was, however, considerable distance between receiving a piece of source code and having a working strategy. The AI wrote the program, the trader copied it into Pine Editor, the compiler complained, and the trader went back to the AI. Sometimes this exchange of pleasantries lasted longer than the development of the trading idea itself.

On November 16, 2026, TradingView gave AI agents access to its native Pine Script compiler and strategy backtesting engine through its own MCP server. Against the relentless stream of artificial intelligence announcements, the news could easily go unnoticed. Yet for the algorithmic trading industry, it may prove considerably more significant than the arrival of another language model.

TradingView has reduced the need for a human intermediary between artificial intelligence and the development environment.

A Compiler at the Other End of the Conversation

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard that allows AI applications to interact with external software. In TradingView's case, the agent communicates with the same computational infrastructure that powers the platform itself.

The language model can now receive feedback directly from the compiler, including line numbers, error positions and warnings. It can correct a program, validate it again and run it against historical market data.

TradingView has introduced eight tools for working with Pine Script:

  • validate_pine_script — validates source code.

  • run_pine_indicator — calculates indicator values.

  • run_pine_backtest — runs a trading strategy backtest.

  • get_pine_script_source — retrieves accessible source code.

  • get_pine_script_info — retrieves script parameters and output information.

  • search_pine_scripts — searches for scripts.

  • create_pine_script and update_pine_script — create and update scripts within the user's account.

When a program is updated, TradingView preserves its previous versions, while code that fails compilation is not saved to the account. Intermediate experiments can be conducted without saving the source code. Other authors' protected and invite-only publications remain inaccessible.

What is particularly noteworthy is that TradingView has not built a separate development environment for artificial intelligence. Instead, it has opened the existing infrastructure that Pine Script developers have been using for years.

Connecting TradingView to Artificial Intelligence

The official MCP server is available here.

The connection uses Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1 authorization. TradingView supports ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, Cursor and other compatible applications. Users simply add the appropriate connector and authorize access through their TradingView account. Detailed instructions are available in the official MCP documentation.

While preparing this article, I connected TradingView to ChatGPT and tried the new integration while developing a strategy based on liquidity sweeps and false breakouts. The purpose was to see how much of the development and testing process could be delegated to the AI agent. The trading idea did not automatically become profitable, but the need to constantly transfer code and test results between applications was considerably reduced. The first noticeable restriction was the number of available requests.

For developers accustomed to working with Pine Editor and Strategy Tester, this way of interacting with the platform may initially feel unfamiliar. After a few iterations, however, it becomes apparent how much time was previously spent on tasks that required neither market knowledge nor any particular programming talent.

Backtesting Is No Longer a Manual Exercise

Throughout the history of financial technology, the cost of computation has repeatedly determined who could afford to employ particular methods of market research. Computing power once reserved for large banks and investment firms gradually found its way onto the retail trader's desk. Now the distance between a trading hypothesis and its computational investigation is shrinking as well.

Through MCP, artificial intelligence can access Strategy Tester statistics: net profit, profit factor, maximum drawdown, total trades, percentage of profitable positions, average profits and losses, and Sharpe and Sortino ratios. The agent can examine individual trades and compare the performance of long and short positions. With an eligible subscription, Deep Backtesting allows research over a specified historical period.

The investigation of a trading system rarely ends with its first successful backtest. It remains necessary to determine how much the results depend on the instrument, timeframe, indicator parameters and prevailing market conditions. Sometimes changing a single number is enough to make a splendid set of statistics disappear.

Until now, such work required considerable involvement from the developer. A sequence of experiments can increasingly be delegated to an AI agent, leaving the human responsible for defining the research question and interpreting the results.

An equally important change concerns the quality of the software itself. One longstanding criticism of language models is their ability to produce entirely nonfunctional programs with disarming confidence. Access to the compiler and execution results makes it possible to uncover many of these mistakes during development. It also becomes easier to establish whether correcting one part of a strategy has inadvertently damaged another.

The quality of AI-assisted software development will improve not only because language models are becoming more capable, but because their mistakes are becoming easier to expose.

There is, of course, another side to this development. Curve-fitting trading strategies to historical data existed long before artificial intelligence. MCP could turn it into an industrial operation. An agent instructed to maximize profitability may discover a magnificent combination of parameters that proves entirely useless outside the period under investigation.

The market is under no obligation to repeat history simply because a computer has learned to study it faster.

Ten Calls Before Breakfast

Beginning November 17, 2026, TradingView applies the following daily MCP usage limits:

The additional AI subscription also carries a limit of 50 requests per minute. Usage limits reflect TradingView’s documentation at publication and may change.

These figures deserve some attention. A single question put to an AI assistant may require several calls to TradingView. Compiling a program, running a backtest, validating a correction and saving a script are separate operations, each consuming part of the overall allowance.

Ten requests may seem perfectly adequate to an occasional chatbot user. A trading system developer could exhaust them before breakfast.

Having removed a human bottleneck from Pine Script development, TradingView has introduced a computational one. The availability of a paid AI subscription also reveals the commercial logic of the arrangement. The company can now sell not only access to analytical tools, but additional computational capacity for artificial intelligence.

In the coming years, the cost of a research iteration may become a factor in its own right when choosing a trading platform.

MetaTrader Is Keeping Pace

TradingView is hardly alone in this endeavor. On July 23, 2026, MetaQuotes introduced MetaTrader 5 Build 6060, with native support for MCP and agentic artificial intelligence. The integration extends across the trading terminal and MetaEditor, allowing AI agents to work with MQL5 source code, compile programs, and test and optimize Expert Advisors. Further details are available in the MetaEditor MCP and AI documentation. Unlike TradingView, MetaTrader's implementation also extends to trading operations. Within four months, two of the largest ecosystems in retail algorithmic trading have given artificial intelligence direct access to development tools previously operated by humans. That is hardly a coincidence.

From Source Code to an Actual Trade

TradingView has drawn a fairly clear distinction between strategy research and trade execution. Its MCP terms of use prohibit using the server for automated trading, trading decisions or connections to trading bots.

For the execution of separately developed and tested strategies, the established mechanism remains trading alerts and webhooks. A Pine Script signal is passed to external software that communicates with a trading platform or broker. This is a separate workflow, not permission to connect TradingView’s MCP server or its alerts to automated trading systems.

As the development of trading algorithms becomes more accessible, demand for execution infrastructure is likely to grow as well. Broker restrictions, position sizing, duplicate signal handling and discrepancies between simulated and actual execution will remain very much a part of the business.

Artificial intelligence considerably simplifies the development of a trading system, but the financial responsibility for its operation still rests with the owner of the trading account.

Storm Clouds Over Alternative Compilers

TradingView's November announcement arrives at a rather inconvenient moment for several young projects born out of Pine Script's limitations. PyneCore and PyneComp offer a route for bringing trading algorithms into Python, while PineForge translates Pine Script v6 into C++ and provides its own backtesting engine, accessible through MCP. PyneCore's developers report compatibility testing across 1,000 published TradingView scripts, while PineForge presents results from nearly 8,000 backtests. These are the projects' own published findings, not independent assessments of their compatibility with the original.

The engineering value of these developments cannot be dismissed. Independent execution, proprietary market datasets and large-scale testing remain attractive propositions, particularly in light of TradingView's daily quotas. Yet as recently as last week, the ability to backtest Pine Script from an AI client without human intervention looked like a substantial competitive advantage. Now the owner of the language itself provides access to the original compiler, historical market data and its native execution environment. Selling independence from TradingView may remain a profitable business. Selling an alternative to its compiler solely for the convenience of AI-assisted development will become considerably harder. Storm clouds are gathering over this young market, and, ironically enough, they have come from TradingView's own cloud infrastructure.

Disclosure: The author uses TradingView as a software platform but has no commercial relationship, sponsorship, partnership or compensation arrangement with TradingView, MetaQuotes, PyneCore, PyneComp or PineForge. This article is neither sponsored nor promotional. No compensation has been received for covering any of the companies or projects mentioned. All references and external links are provided solely for readers' convenience and independent research.

data.title: Why The Biggest IPO Ever Matters For Gold Investors
data.description:
On October 29, I wrote that when gold falls on supportive news, the sellers are in control. Gold is about $300 lower now.

At the moment of writing these words, December gold futures trade near $3,720, after moving down to $3,694.50 overnight, their lowest level since September 2, 2025. Silver futures trade near $45, and the GDXJ, the ETF for junior mining stocks, closed at $90.07 on Wednesday, its lowest close since November 2025. Meanwhile, the stock futures are higher ahead of the debut of Anthropic, whose IPO is the biggest on record.

The rule about the sellers works in the stock market too, and Wednesday showed it. 

Stocks Ignored the Best News of the Week

On October 29, when December gold futures traded near $4,033, I wrote: "When gold falls on a day that should support it, the sellers are in control. In my view, this is bearish information." Since then, gold has declined by about 8 percent.

On Wednesday, stocks had every reason to rally. Nvidia's (NVDA) revenue rose 103 percent from a year earlier and beat expectations; Target (TGT) and Lowe's (LOW) beat expectations as well, oil fell, and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 5.06 percent. The S&P 500 fell anyway. It lost 0.23 percent, to 7,323.63, its fifth decline in a row and its lowest close since July 29. The sellers are in control of stocks too, and this matters for the stock market's relationship with gold, because the miners are stocks as well.

It's also notable that the S&P 500 isn't soaring from its lows the way it did before. In late July, it gained 1.66 percent on the day after its July 29 close. In early November, it soared on the third day: after the lows of November 5 and 6, it gained 2.35 percent on November 9. This morning, the S&P 500 futures are up about 1.2 percent, which isn't much after five declines in a row.

Tech stocks are holding up better. On Wednesday, the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.42 percent, while the S&P 500 lost 0.23 percent, and this morning, the Nasdaq 100 futures are up about 2 percent. In my view, this could be based on the hype around Anthropic's (ANT) IPO, and it could be overstated.

That hype deserves a closer look, because hyped listings have a track record. 

What Hyped Listings Have Told Us About Tops

On Wednesday evening, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the $70-78 range, at a valuation of about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. Its shares start trading on Nasdaq today under the ticker ANT.

SpaceX (SPCX) is the freshest example of what came next in such cases. It priced its IPO at $135 on June 11 and reached $225.64 on June 16, its third day of trading. That was the top. By mid-July, SpaceX traded below its IPO price, and on Wednesday, it closed at $143.50, about 36 percent below the June high.

Silver did the same in 2006, when the first big silver ETF was launched. The iShares Silver Trust (SLV) started trading on April 28, 2006. Silver kept rallying for less than two weeks, and the gain was less than 20 percent. It topped on May 11, and within about a month, it fell about 35 percent.

There are more examples. Palm's (PALMV) IPO in March 2000 came 6 trading days before the Nasdaq's record close at the peak of the dot-com bubble, and the index then lost 78 percent. Rivian's (RIVN) IPO in November 2021 came 7 trading days before the Nasdaq's record close of that cycle.

Not every hyped listing marks the top of the entire market. After SpaceX's IPO, the Nasdaq Composite kept rising until its October 6 record. Anthropic, though, is listing into a market that's already falling: the Nasdaq 100 closed on Wednesday about 13 percent below its October 6 record, and Nvidia closed at its lowest level since June 2025 despite beating expectations. 

Why Hyped Listings Tend to Come Near Tops

There are three reasons. The first is new supply. Anthropic's IPO and private placement brought $107.3 billion of new shares to the market, five months after SpaceX's $75 billion IPO set the previous record, and to buy the new shares, many investors sell other stocks. The second is that insiders choose when to sell. Companies and their early investors go public when buyers are willing to pay the most, which is why IPOs cluster after strong markets. The third is that nobody might be left to buy. Those who want the hyped stock buy it in the first days, and after that, the sellers take over.

In my view, this IPO might be happening at the peak of the AI hype or right after it peaked, and it could be the final moment when the enthusiasm peaks. Anthropic's valuation of about $1.5 trillion is up from $965 billion in its private funding round in May. It might not be realistic, and investors might realize that and sell the stock, even though AI technology is revolutionary.

If that happens, the miners are likely to feel it first. 

Why the Miners Fall Harder

When stocks decline, the mining stocks tend to fall more than gold, because investors sell them as stocks first and as gold proxies second. On Wednesday, the GDXJ fell 6.02 percent, almost twice as much as gold, on a day when the S&P 500 lost only 0.23 percent.

On October 26, after gold slipped below $4,000, I wrote: "Until the miners start rising on gold's down days, or at least falling less than gold, I think the decline in the sector has further to go." Since then, the GDXJ has lost about 9 percent, and gold about 7 percent. The miners are still falling more than gold, and on Wednesday, the GDXJ broke down to new 2026 lows, also in terms of the closing prices.

Gold itself reached an important level overnight. 

Gold Reaches Its Declining Support Line

On September 10, when gold traded near $4,400, I wrote that a daily close below the neckline of gold's head-and-shoulders top, then near $4,320, "would complete the formation with its target below $4,000." Since then, gold has declined by about 15 percent.

Now, gold has moved down to its declining support line, and such gold support levels often slow a decline, so a pause is possible here, also in silver and the mining stocks.

One of my Gold Trading Alerts subscribers asked in the comments whether I expect any rally attempts before gold reaches about $3,500. It's a good question, and I'm happy to answer it here as well. In short, a pause is possible here, but I don't expect a meaningful rally before the next leg lower. In April 2013, no consolidation followed the breakdown: gold crashed 10.8 percent to its April 16 low, and the 12.6 percent correction came only after that. In my view, a sizable gold price correction is more likely to start from lower prices than from current prices. On a side note, I just updated my final downside target for gold - $3,500 is just the first one.

Before I sum up, there's one more thing worth celebrating today. 

Happy International Men's Day

Today, November 19, is International Men's Day. Dr. Jerome Teelucksingh from Trinidad and Tobago first celebrated it in 1999, and it's now marked in more than 80 countries. The day celebrates the positive value that men bring to the world, their families and their communities, and this year's theme is "The Future Is Everyone."

To all the men reading this: Happy International Men's Day! I wish you good health, strength and plenty of time with the people who matter most to you. If there's a check-up that you've been postponing, today is a good day to book it. You are important. And if that doesn’t convince you, think of your body as a business asset – you don’t want it to depreciate too fast… And to all the women reading this: thank you for celebrating with us. 

Where This Leaves Us

The stock market ignored the best news of the week, and today, the biggest IPO on record debuts into a market that's already falling. Hyped listings have often come near tops, and when stocks decline, the miners tend to fall harder than gold. Gold reached its declining support line, so a pause is possible here, but in my view, gold is likely to decline to at least $3,500. In today's Gold Trading Alert, I also updated my long-term gold chart and my view on where this decline is most likely to end, and I described my plan for the next two trades.

When the last buyers are in, the hype ends, and the miners are usually the first to feel it.

data.title: Yen Threatens Key Level Ahead Of Inflation Data
data.description:
The USDJPY is just shy of the 160 level it touched last week, potentially triggering an intervention by Japanese authorities to arrest weakness in their currency. It’s a crucial juncture ahead of key data that will be decisive for the BOJ’s policy.

Investors are betting that Japan’s central bank won’t keep pace with a more hawkish Fed, which will widen the interest-rate gap between the currencies. The carry trade becomes increasingly interesting as the gap widens, but the potential for intervention by Japanese authorities could limit the upside. That is, unless there is a substantial shift in the underlying data that would encourage traders to challenge the financial authorities trying to slow the rise in the USDJPY.

The BOJ’s Inflation Problem

Japanese policymakers are concerned about their currency weakening too fast, as it would disrupt its trade-dependent economy. The main cause is that the BOJ maintains the lowest borrowing rates among the major currencies, making it profitable for traders to sell yen to buy other currencies. This is a growing problem as other central banks are poised to raise rates in December to address energy-induced inflationary pressures. (Australia’s RBA being a notable exception, but having already the highest rates among the majors.)

The way to deal with this problem is for the BOJ to raise rates along with its counterparts. But to justify such a move, there needs to be inflationary pressure, and Japan’s sluggish economy and high savings rates have kept inflation relatively low in the island nation. In fact, it was last reported practically on target, and if it continues to underperform, it could undermine the case for further rate hikes.

What the Market Is Looking For

On Friday, Japan will report its October CPI data, and it is expected to show headline CPI at 2.0%, down from 2.1% a month earlier. The slight downward variation is expected to be attributed to easing energy prices. The so-called “core core” rate (excluding energy and food costs, equivalent to other countries’ “core”) is projected to remain unchanged at 2.4%.

With the core rate above target, the BOJ has an excuse to pursue or at least signal a hawkish stance. So, if the core rate were to decline, it could embolden the market to weaken the yen. Likewise, if the headline inflation rate falls substantially below target, it could shake the BOJ’s resolve to raise rates.

What Are the Odds of a BOJ Hike?

At the moment, the market is pricing in an 86% chance of a December BOJ rate hike, allowing it to keep pace with the Fed and ECB, both of which are also expected to raise rates at the same time. If that dynamic persists, it would be easier for Japanese authorities to keep a lid on the USDJPY.

Hotter-than-expected inflation would raise the odds of a rate hike, but the market is already fairly confident in one, reducing the potential impact. Since the recent move higher in USDJPY is mostly due to the dollar, it’s unlikely the currency pair will reverse substantially on Japanese data. This means the potential for a bigger surprise is to the upside (weaker yen).

data.title: Nasdaq 100 Jumps Ahead Of Anthropic Debut
data.description:
US equity futures are pointing higher across the board, with the Nasdaq 100 leading the advance with a 2% rise, as semiconductor stocks benefit from renewed enthusiasm around artificial intelligence. The index found decent support ahead of Anthropic’s (ANT) debut, with Nvidia (NVDA)’s earnings results also helping to stabilise sentiment. The recovery is certainly a welcome development after a troubling week for financial markets, with equities, gold, silver and Bitcoin (BTC.X) all coming under significant selling pressure.

So, is this an early sign that risk appetite is returning, or are we simply seeing a temporary rebound in the Nasdaq 100 futures within a broader bearish market? I think it is far too early for the bulls to declare victory until we see a more convincing sign of a market bottom.

All eyes on Anthropic

Anthropic has priced its shares at $83, raising $81.3 billion in what is reportedly the largest IPO on record. The stock is due to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT, with the company carrying a valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion.

Its sheer size is expected to put it on course for accelerated inclusion in several major indices, including the Nasdaq 100, as early as late November or December. That could generate substantial demand from passive funds tracking those benchmarks. The S&P 500, however, is likely to be a longer wait, given its eligibility requirements, including a sufficient period of public trading and sustained GAAP profitability.

The IPO provides another focal point for a technology sector that has struggled to maintain its earlier momentum.  Will Anthropic be among the biggest stock gainers today, or will it get sold?

US equities have weathered the storm for now, but choppy waters ahead

US equities have endured a difficult few sessions, yet their resilience remains striking when compared with the much steeper declines in Bitcoin, silver and several major Asian equity markets. That said, relative outperformance should not be confused with immunity to a broader correction. Despite today’s bounce, the Nasdaq 100 remains well below its October peak, while underlying vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly difficult to overlook.

There are several reasons why Wall Street has held up better than other markets. Unlike in 2022, when aggressive Federal Reserve tightening triggered a widespread repricing of risk, the US economy has remained relatively resilient. Corporate earnings have also provided a degree of protection, while the enormous investment flowing into AI infrastructure continues to support expectations for future growth.

Nvidia’s latest results have helped reinforce that narrative, easing concerns that the AI investment cycle might be approaching a turning point. But questions over the eventual returns on such substantial capital expenditure have not gone away. With valuations elevated, even modest disappointments in corporate guidance could prompt a more meaningful reassessment of the sector.

Monetary policy presents another potential headwind. Further evidence of persistent inflation could strengthen expectations of additional Fed tightening, pushing Treasury yields higher and making expensive equity valuations harder to justify.

For now, economic resilience, earnings growth and the AI investment boom are providing Wall Street with important support. Anthropic’s debut may offer a fresh catalyst for technology shares, but it does little to resolve the broader questions surrounding valuations and the sustainability of AI-related spending. The risk of a deeper correction should not be dismissed.

Nasdaq 100 technical analysis

The Nasdaq 100 was attempting to end a four-day losing streak, gaining more than 2% at the time of writing.

For now, I would approach this recovery with a degree of caution. Markets have been particularly choppy of late, and several major indices have already broken through important technical levels. The Nasdaq 100, for instance, has moved below its 200-day moving average recently, as you can see on the chart.

On the upside, initial resistance comes in between 27,850 and 28,230. This is an important technical area where several previous support and resistance levels converge, alongside the 200-day moving average and a short-term bearish trend line.

A decisive move back above this zone would be an encouraging bullish signal, potentially opening the door to further technical buying towards the 28,815 to 29,000 support-turned-resistance area. That is the next significant resistance zone, and a break above it would considerably improve the technical outlook.

On the downside, initial support is seen around 27,500, which marks Tuesday’s high.

Below there, we have 27,200. This is particularly important as it marks the late-July low, which was temporarily breached on a couple of occasions in early November and again earlier this week before the index recovered.

If the Nasdaq falls back below 27,200 and starts holding beneath that level, the technical picture would deteriorate considerably, increasing the risk of another leg lower.

Further down, the next major support zone comes in between 26,350 and 26,400, marking previous highs from late last year and early this year. This zone was tested earlier this month, providing a solid bounce.

So, has the market bottomed?

Potentially, but I wouldn’t jump on the bullish bandwagon just yet. We need to see further evidence before becoming confident that a sustainable bottom is in place. Until then, I would treat this as a level-to-level market, with the next few sessions potentially providing more clarity. Judging by price action elsewhere in financial markets, I would be extra careful to chase the market higher.

data.title: Bigger Rug, Bigger Rug Pull
data.description:
Last Friday, we described that day’s activity as a “rug pull.”  On that day, we saw stocks rise in the pre-market and on the open, then sink quickly afterwards.  Today, we’re seeing something similar, though after a much bigger early rally.  Traders were clearly enthusiastic about the prospects for the much-awaited IPO[i] (it has still not opened as I type this), but that stock’s coattails were not long enough to drag the whole market along with it this morning.

The charts below show the dramatic moves in both ES (E-Mini S&P 500) and NQ (Nasdaq 100 E-Mini) December Futures.  At their highs, ES was up about 1.4% around 6:55 ET, and NQ was up about 2.4% around 9:50. Soon afterwards, those gains reversed quite abruptly.  The S&P 500 (SPX) gravitated once again toward the 7,300 level that has provided support over the past three sessions, while the Nasdaq 100 (NDX) spent very little time in negative territory.

ES December Futures, 2 Days, 2 Minute Candles

NQ December Futures, 2 Days, 2 Minute Candles

The pre-market bounce was easy to explain.  A supersized deal reaffirmed, at least for now, enthusiasm for the artificial intelligence theme that has propelled stocks over the past four years.  There was also a belief that many investors were raising cash to participate in the new issue, so there was hope that those who did not receive their desired allocations would put money back to work in other stocks. 

The rationale for the quick drop is less apparent.  It seems to be merely the latest round of “sell the rally” behavior that has pervaded market activity this month.  Around 11:30 ET, NYSE decliners led advancers by roughly 3:1, and the technology sector was the only SPX sector showing gains.  Within SPX, there were more than 250 net decliners. 

OK, while I was typing, the IPO began trading and stocks took another leg lower – a big one!  I updated the charts above with data from shortly after noon ET.  The drop was quick, stunning, and meaningful.  It appears that traders were waiting for the deal to begin trading to unleash another bout of selling, and once SPX broke through its recent support, that led to another round of sharp declines.

As of 12:18 ET, NYSE decliners are leading by a 4:1 ratio and SPX has 424 net decliners among its 500 stocks.   All 11 SPX sectors are lower, with only energy showing a loss of less than 1%.  What started as a hopeful day for many has turned into a significant disappointment. 

Barring a major turnaround this afternoon, we are looking at the type of day that some view as ominous.  With higher highs and lower lows than the prior day, SPX and NDX are potentially forming outside reversals.  Who knows, though?  SPX has rallied about 50 points since I posted the graphs above.  Perhaps the second leg lower was the result of stop-loss orders that had little follow-through.  Buckle up for the volatility.

[i] I think you know what stock I’m referred to, but I’m not allowed to discuss it until the selling syndicate closes.

data.title: AI Is Changing How Medicines Are Discovered. These 4 Stocks Are Positioned to Benefit (ANT, MEDS, RXRX, SDGR)
data.description:
Naples, FL, November 20th, 2026, FinanceWire


AI is increasingly becoming part of the drug discovery process, with researchers exploring how machine learning can identify therapeutic targets, design molecules, and accelerate the development of new treatments. The technology could help address some of the pharmaceutical industry's longstanding challenges, including lengthy development timelines, high research costs, and the difficulty of identifying promising drug candidates. Recent developments are highlighting the growing commercial potential of AI-driven drug discovery, as companies push beyond theoretical applications and begin demonstrating how these tools can contribute to actual pharmaceutical research.

Anthropic recently outlined how its AI models are being used across drug development, detailing partnerships with six organizations working to develop new medicines. The applications range from generating roughly 35,000 antibody designs for a food allergy treatment to improving cancer-targeting molecules and reducing manufacturing documentation review time by 89% at Enveda. Bristol Myers Squibb is also using Claude to assess early-stage clinical trial plans.

The announcement highlights AI's expanding role across drug discovery and development, from identifying targets and designing molecules to supporting clinical research. Several publicly traded companies are approaching this emerging field from different angles. Here are four stocks to take a closer look at.

DataMEDS AI, Inc. (NASDAQ:MEDS) is a Tampa, Florida-based healthcare company that integrates its health information technology and physical infrastructure with its EinsteinRx artificial intelligence platform and PharmacyChain blockchain-enabled smart contracts platform. The company recently announced that its wholly owned subsidiary Helomics, a CLIA-certified cancer diagnostics laboratory that DataMEDS acquired in September, entered a cancer target discovery and drug candidate optimization partnership with DiaGen.ai, an AI-driven drug discovery company based in Vancouver, Canada. Under the partnership, DiaGen gains access to the Helomics biobank, which holds more than 70,000 primary tumor biopsies, including more than 50,000 gynecologic cancer samples collected over nearly three decades.

The companies will first focus on validating 15 cytotoxic peptides that showed in vitro proof of concept in breast cancer cell lines, including triple-negative breast cancer. DiaGen will use its BLACKCOMB AI small-molecule design platform to build a library of drug candidates, Helomics will run the preclinical validation work on cell lines and primary tumors, and the two companies will jointly own the intellectual property that results. As part of the agreement, DataMEDS will issue 630,000 common shares to DiaGen, equal to 9.9% of its shares outstanding at the time of the agreement, and DiaGen will issue 9.9% of its fully diluted common shares to DataMEDS. The total value of the transaction is expected to be $1.5 million in cash and in-kind contributions through completion of project milestones.

DataMEDS has been active on other fronts as well. Its pharmacy subsidiary, Corexa Pharmacy, recently announced its first commercial sale of compounded peptides under the FDA's enforcement discretion policy, and the company reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $2.7 million, up 50% from $1.8 million in the second quarter, driven primarily by growth in Corexa Pharmacy drug dispensing. In November, DataMEDS also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with a Florida-based HMO to deploy its Health Lives Here mobile app to more than 25,000 members, with definitive agreements expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) is a San Francisco-based AI company founded in 2021 by siblings Dario Amodei, its CEO, and Daniela Amodei, its president, and it is structured as a public benefit corporation. Anthropic launched its Claude family of AI models commercially in early 2023, and businesses and individuals use Claude for tasks across industries, including coding, medicine, law, and science. The company sells Claude to enterprise customers and to individual subscribers, and its registration statement reported more than 11,900 customers generating $100,000 or more in trailing 12-month revenue as of September 30, 2026.

In January, Anthropic introduced Claude for Healthcare, a set of tools for health systems, insurers, and patients that runs on HIPAA-ready infrastructure, connects Claude to industry databases and medical coding systems, and lets individual users connect their own health records. Anthropic has since extended Claude further into life sciences, rolling out Claude Science, an AI workbench for researchers, and beginning drug discovery programs of its own, including through its acquisition of Mithril Medicine, a company developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy.

Anthropic recently launched the roadshow for an initial public offering of Class A common stock and applied to list the shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.

Schrödinger, Inc. (NASDAQ:SDGR) is a computational drug discovery company that sells software built on a physics-based platform for molecular discovery and also runs its own drug discovery programs and collaborations. The company recently announced third-quarter 2026 results, reporting annual contract value of $44.7 million, up 17% from a year earlier, and trailing four-quarter annual contract value of $214 million, along with drug discovery revenue of $24 million. Schrödinger also increased its full-year 2026 guidance for annual contract value and drug discovery revenue.

In September, Schrödinger contributed two early-stage small-molecule programs, SDGR-4594 and SDGR-8139, to Tectora Therapeutics in connection with Tectora's $55 million Series A financing, in exchange for an equity stake and eligibility for future milestones. Earlier this year, the company launched an early access version of Bunsen, an agentic AI co-scientist designed to plan and run molecular discovery workflows on its platform.

Recursion Pharmaceuticals (NASDAQ:RXRX) is a clinical-stage biotechnology company that uses AI to discover and develop medicines, with a pipeline focused on oncology and rare diseases. The company recently announced its third-quarter 2026 results, reporting revenue of $18.55 million compared with $5.18 million a year earlier, driven mainly by a $10 million milestone payment from its collaboration with Sanofi, and a net loss of $119.0 million compared with $162.3 million in the same quarter last year. Recursion also said it extended its cash runway into 2029.

The company also presented new Phase 2 data for REC-4881 in familial adenomatous polyposis, a hereditary condition associated with gastrointestinal cancer risk. After 12 weeks of treatment, 87% of evaluable patients had reductions in total polyp burden, with a median reduction of 47%, and about one-third reached reductions of at least 65%. Recursion expects to begin a registrational study in the second half of 2027, pending discussions with the FDA. Separately, Sanofi has optioned a development candidate from the collaboration, and Genentech exercised its first Validated Target Option under the neuroscience collaboration.

Bank of America Fund Manager Survey Update

On Tuesday, we put out a summary of the monthly Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey. This month, they surveyed 169 institutional managers with ~$461B in AUM:

Here were the 5 key points:

1) Fund managers piled back into the consumer in November, with combined allocation to discretionary + staples jumping 28 ppts to a net 38% underweight from a net 66% underweight last month, the biggest monthly increase since June 2006. Discretionary moved to a net 20% underweight from a net 34% underweight, while staples climbed to a net 18% underweight from a net 32% underweight. We have spent months pounding the table on buying anything with a fork or a sneaker (restaurants, apparel, footwear, etc.), with opinion now following trend. Even after the rotation, discretionary still sits 0.8 standard deviations below its long-term average and staples 1.0 standard deviations below, leaving plenty of room to work higher.

2) Fund managers cut their technology allocation by 25 ppts to a net 12% overweight from a net 37% overweight last month, the biggest monthly reduction since June 2006, leaving positioning 0.5 standard deviations below its long-term average. The cut comes just one month after managers piled into their most overweight tech position since August 2020, with everyone swept up in the AI trade just in time for it to roll over.

3) Inflation expectations have inflected lower, with a net 32% of fund managers now expecting lower global CPI in 12 months’ time (vs. net 5% last month), the lowest inflation expectations since October 2024. Fears of a second wave of inflation have faded along with them, slipping to just 14% as a tail risk.

4) A majority of fund managers (52%) now expect an AI hyperscaler to announce a capex cut over the next six months, up from 30% last month and just 14% in September, while those expecting no cuts fell to 40%. The message to hyperscalers is clear, with a record net 38% saying companies are overinvesting and just 16% wanting them to boost capex (the lowest since May 2020), while AI hyperscaler bonds remain the most likely source of a systemic credit event (38%).

5) “Long global semiconductors” remains the most crowded trade at 39%, though that share has fallen steadily from a record 82% in July 2026. Behind it, “short China stocks” has popped up as the second most crowded trade at 14%, a consensus we are happy to take the other side of. We continue to see China as the cheapest way to play AI globally, with BABA effectively serving as a Chinese AI ETF while also acting as a toll taker on the Chinese consumer recovery.

Advance Auto Parts Update

For newer readers, here’s a quick overview of the key drivers behind our thesis on Advance Auto Parts, the long-neglected auto parts retailer undergoing a back-to-basics turnaround with substantial margin recovery still ahead:

Company Overview

  • Leading automotive aftermarket parts retailer founded in 1929; headquartered in Raleigh, NC

  • Blended-box model serving Pro (~50% of sales) and DIY (~50%) from the same locations

  • 4,087 Advance Auto Parts stores + 238 Carquest stores as of Q3 2026 (4,325 total); #3 U.S. player behind O’Reilly and AutoZone

  • Also services 787 independently owned Carquest branded stores across the US, Canada, Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, and various Caribbean islands

  • 90% of sales from maintenance and break-fix categories

  • Net sales from continuing operations ~$8.6B in FY2025

  • Revenue mix: parts and batteries 63%, accessories and chemicals 22%, engine maintenance 14%

  • Structural tailwinds: average U.S. vehicle age at a record 12.8 years in 2025 (estimated 13.0 years in 2026), growing vehicle base, and rising miles traveled supporting steady 3.5%+ industry growth (DIFM outpacing DIY)

  • U.S. light-duty vehicle parc of 289M today, up from 263M in 2016 and projected to exceed 301M by 2029

  • More than 110M vehicles now sit in the prime aftermarket service window of 6 to 14 years, nearly 38% of the fleet, with S&P Global expecting that share to reach ~40% by 2028

  • Total vehicle miles traveled rebounded to 3.34T after troughing in 2021

  • $160B TAM with AAP holding just over 5% share; the big 3 hold under 30% of the industry, leaving plenty of share to be gained

  • Shares still down >80% from 2022 highs (~$240), trading at 2010 levels

Management

  • CEO Shane O’Kelly (since August 2023): proven supply chain and operations leader with 30+ years in distribution and logistics

  • Former CEO of HD Supply ($8B+ business sold to Home Depot), CEO of PetroChoice (world’s largest lubricant distributor), and 7-year U.S. Army officer

  • CFO Ryan Grimsland (late 2023): ~17 years at Lowe’s

  • Board additions: Tom Seboldt (30+ years at O’Reilly), Gregory Smith (Goodyear operations, Walmart supply chain), Brett Windom (former Pep Boys CEO)

WorldPac Sale

  • Sold WorldPac wholesale/import parts business to Carlyle for $1.5B cash (announced August 2024, closed November 2024)

  • Net proceeds ~$1.45B after taxes and fees; tax liability came in ~$200M lower than expected

  • Proceeds used for debt reduction: transformed $1.3B net debt (end-2023) into ~$80M net cash by end-2024

  • Leverage taken down from >4x to 2.2x at end of Q3 2026 (within target range of 2x to 2.5x), vs. 2.1x in Q2 2026

  • $3.1B of cash on the balance sheet against $3.4B of debt at end of Q3 2026 ($349M of 1.75% notes due October 2027 now current)

  • Repurchased and retired ~$30M of principal on the 2028 senior notes in Q2 2026, the first debt reduction since the WorldPac paydown; Moody’s and S&P both moved to a stable outlook during the quarter (investment grade remains 3 notches away at Moody’s, 2 at S&P)

  • Removes lower-margin wholesale drag; simplifies focus on core retail/Pro blended-box model with solvency risk off the table

Margin Expansion

  • Operating margins bottomed in FY2024 at just 0.4% of net sales, the weakest in 20+ years due to prior expansion missteps, supply chain inefficiencies, and under-investment in core operations

  • Trailing peers dramatically: AutoZone/O’Reilly at ~19-20%; AAP historically maintained 9-11% before missteps

  • Productivity review identifies >500 bps of margin opportunity

  • FY2025 adjusted operating margin of 2.5% (+213 bps Y/Y from near-breakeven)

  • Q3 2026 adjusted operating margin of 4.5% (+10 bps Y/Y) on a negative comp, with adjusted operating income of $91M ahead of consensus $88.4M; excluding Q2 tariff refunds, one of the strongest margin quarters since the strategic plan began; YTD adjusted operating margin of 4.6% vs. 2.2% last year

  • Q3 2026 adjusted gross margin of 44.7% (-16 bps Y/Y) on ~40 bps of DIY mix, fuel, and supply chain deleverage plus ~20 bps of product mix into motor oil, partially offset by ~40 bps of net LIFO benefit; YTD 45.3% (+150 bps Y/Y), with merchandising initiatives contributing ~100 bps of gross margin expansion YTD

  • Not yet fully passing commodity cost inflation through to customers, viewing much of the pressure as transitory; rational fast follower on pricing, not leading the market higher or lower

  • Q3 2026 adjusted SG&A of 40.2% of net sales, 26 bps of leverage Y/Y with dollars down ~2%; productivity found in non-customer-facing areas (indirect spend, cloud consolidation) reinvested in the frontline

  • FY2026 guidance: adjusted operating margin narrowed to 4.0-4.3% from 3.8-4.5% (4.15% midpoint reaffirmed, +150+ bps)

  • Management expects at least another 100+ bps expansion in FY2027, a third straight year of 100+ bps expansion, driven by merchandising, labor productivity, and supply chain (incl. 20+ bps from transportation); built off the H2 2026 base (~3.65%) rather than the full year given ~30 bps of non-repeating tariff refunds and ~50 bps of fuel/deleverage pressure lingering into H1 2027, implying ~4.7%

  • SG&A expected to grow roughly in line with sales in FY2027 as productivity savings are reinvested in stores, hubs, and frontline labor, leaving gross margin as the main driver of incremental expansion

  • Medium-term target: 7% adjusted operating margin still viewed as appropriate, though pushed out as the original plan assumed steady low-single-digit comps; implies ~$630M operating income on $9B sales

  • Last time AAP had operating income in the $600M range (2018-2022), EPS was $5.75-$7.70 and shares reached $182-$244 (with 10%+ higher share count)

  • Consensus cut post-print to ~4.53% for FY2027 and ~5.0% for FY2028, right around management’s framework; EPS of $3.47 in FY2027 (+20.1% Y/Y) and $4.14 in FY2028 (+19.1% Y/Y) on top-line growth of 2.1% and 2.4%

  • At 7% on ~$9B, ~$630M of operating income supports close to $7 per share of normalized earnings power, more than double the current run-rate

Supply Chain Overhaul

  • Prolonged underperformance stems from supply chain inefficiencies (failure to properly integrate after the Carquest and now-divested WorldPac acquisitions in 2014)

  • DC consolidation completed in Q2 2026: down to 15 DCs on a single unified warehouse management system, from nearly 40 of varying sizes and systems when the project began; 12-13 long-term

  • Market hubs rollout (hub-and-spoke network modeled after AutoZone and O’Reilly): 46 hubs at end of Q3 2026 (up from 0 at end-2023); opened 14 in 2025 vs. prior target of 10

  • FY2026 plan of 15-20 reaffirmed (13 opened through Q3), targeting ~50 by year-end and ~60 by mid-2027

  • Hubs carry ~85K SKUs with 5x+ the backroom hard parts space of an average store and multiple same-day delivery runs to surrounding stores; ~100 bps comp uplift in served locations; 70%+ of stores inside a hub ecosystem by end-2026, majority of stores by mid-2027

  • Greenfield hubs outperforming the converted Carquest DC locations given better retail positioning

  • Parts availability up from low-90s% to 96-97% (target: high-90s%)

  • Delivery times to Pro customers down from 50+ minutes to consistently under 40 minutes (target: 30-40 minutes)

  • Unified warehouse management system delivering >50 bps of annualized cost savings from H2 2025 onward

  • Driving key DC process improvements (receiving, put-away, inbound/outbound) across all DCs in stages through mid-2027 to lower handling costs, improve shipment accuracy, and shorten lead times; productivity savings expected to drive gross margin expansion in FY2027 and beyond

  • Carrier contracts bid with volume consolidating into 70% fewer carriers, expected to generate 20+ bps of cost savings even in a flattish sales environment, supporting FY2027 margins; first phase of a broader transportation opportunity

  • Formed a dedicated team in Q3 2026 to build a multi-year inventory planning and allocation roadmap targeting working capital efficiency

Improved Store Operations

  • Closed >700 underperforming stores (523 corporate + 204 independent) in 2025, representing a 10% reduction in corporate stores and a 20% cut in U.S. independent locations; saved ~$70M in operating costs

  • 75% of the footprint now in #1 or #2 density markets

  • Upgraded >1,600 stores in FY2025 (paint, HVAC, signage, racking) vs. 440 in FY2024; plan 1,000+ in FY2026

  • New assortment framework rolled out to top 50 DMAs (~70% of sales); initial ~50 bps comp uplift with expanded assortment of +100K SKUs in FY2025 and ~100K added YTD in FY2026, with AI-enabled tools aligning inventory to local demand

  • On schedule to fully deploy the new pricing framework across both DIY and Pro by year-end 2026, improving visibility into competitive pricing actions and enabling precise market-based pricing, alongside tighter discipline around store-level promotions

  • Opened 35 new stores in FY2025; FY2026 plan cut to 30-35 from 40-45 as capital shifts toward market hubs (26 opened and 6 closed through Q3)

  • Newly launched ARGOS owned brand (motor oil, expanded into hydraulic oils, antifreeze, performance chemicals, washer fluid) now AAP’s highest unit-selling motor oil, with further category expansion underway as the DIY consumer trades toward value

  • Modernized DIY loyalty program “Advance Rewards” launched in Q1 2026 (replacing Speed Perks), driving higher new member sign-ups, program penetration, and total transactions from loyalty members

  • Focus on better training, frontline workers who know auto parts, and improved customer service; NPS above 80 in Q3 2026 vs. the high 70s in Q2 and high 60s last year, with in-store attachment rates in the mid-30s from ~30%

  • Completed an independent study of store task execution in Q2 2026 to update labor standards left unchanged for over a decade, now modernizing workforce management tools to shift task hours to selling hours

  • Zebra devices now in every store; ReliaScan check-engine diagnostic tool (free customer service) deployed across most stores in Q3 2026

Return to Growth

  • FY2025 comp sales +0.8%, the first positive comp after 3 straight years of declines; FY2026 on track for back-to-back years of positive comps (YTD +0.8%)

  • Q3 2026 comp sales -1.2% vs. consensus +0.4% and -0.5% in Q2, but trends improved through the quarter off the late-Q2 trough (~-3%): ~-2% in the first 8 weeks before turning positive in the final 4, driven by transactions as store service execution and value messaging improved

  • Pro led the quarter at +low-single digits, positive every month and accelerating to ~+3% in the final 4 weeks

  • Deliberate pivot toward Main Street Pro (small independent repair shops), the largest Pro segment at ~80% of Pro sales, which ran ~100 bps ahead of overall Pro on new customer acquisition and existing customers moving into higher weekly spending tiers

  • Main Street is a higher-quality, more productive sale than national accounts, with better flow-through supporting margins and FCF; rationalization of lower-margin national accounts (~100 bps Pro headwind, ~50 bps to total sales) largely cycled by early Q1 2027, with mix now in line with the industry

  • Two levers for Main Street growth: winning new shops from the hundreds of thousands of 1-4 bay independents nationwide, and moving existing customers up the call list (e.g. $500/week to $1,000-$2,000+) by cross-selling categories

  • Main Street push supported by improved parts availability, sub-40-minute delivery, hundreds of outside sales reps visiting shops daily, and the TechNet program (nationwide repair warranty that lets independents compete like scale players); account segmentation being enhanced and service territories reorganized to capture more growth

  • DIY declined low-single digits as low-to-middle income households stayed stretched by persistent inflation and higher gas prices, but recovered from ~-7% in late Q2 and -4%+ in the first 8 weeks of Q3 to low-single-digit declines in the final 4 weeks; units per transaction up low-single digits with average ticket growth above same-SKU inflation

  • DIY is AAP’s highest-margin channel, so any recovery brings a mix tailwind to margins

  • Maintenance and failure categories (motor oil, batteries, filters, wipers) led while hard parts lagged as value-conscious consumers deferred larger repairs; maintenance spending can only be put off so long

  • DIY action plan: sharper value messaging, Advance Rewards loyalty, paid search optimization, ReliaScan diagnostics, and ARGOS private label for the value-seeking customer

  • Macro turning: gas prices rolled over in late September, down ~$0.70/gallon from the peak to $3.78 (8-month low); energy eats up 17.4% of pre-tax income for the bottom quintile (bulk of it gasoline) vs. 2.7% for the top; lower-income households led October card spending growth (+5.9%, BofA) with holiday spending up ~9% Y/Y; October retail sales +6.8% Y/Y (strongest since October 2022)

  • Consumer sentiment washed out at 48 in October vs. the 44.8 May low; last nine sentiment troughs averaged 24.1% S&P 500 returns over the following 12 months

  • Same-SKU inflation ~4% (motor oil ~100 bps), with AAP a rational fast follower on pricing, not leading the market higher or lower

  • FY2026 guidance: comp sales lowered to ~+1% from +1-2%, implying accelerating comps in Q4; Q4 net sales ~+1% Y/Y ex-53rd week; early Q4 DIY flattish with Pro accelerating to low-to-mid single digits

  • Long-term: low-single-digit comps; target $9B net sales by FY2027

Key Financials + Valuation

  • FY2025 adjusted EPS: $2.26

  • Q3 2026 adjusted EPS: $0.79 vs. consensus $0.78 and $0.92 last year (higher adjusted tax rate); YTD adjusted EPS $2.59 vs. $1.40

  • FY2026 guidance: net sales ~$8.50B (from $8.485-$8.575B), adjusted EPS narrowed to $2.75-$3.10 from $2.60-$3.30 (consensus $2.96), FCF raised to ~$150M from ~$100M, ~$105M of interest income (up $5M) against ~$210M of interest expense; capex ~$300M (up from $252M in FY2025) for new hubs, new stores, store upgrades, and in-store technology

  • YTD free cash flow of +$109M vs. an outflow of $277M last year, the first positive year-to-date FCF in two years; YTD operating cash flow of +$311M vs. -$118M, absorbing capex of $202M vs. $159M

  • FY2026 FCF target raised 50% to ~$150M (>$400M Y/Y improvement), which would mark the first full year of positive free cash flow since FY2022; mgmt does not expect FCF to go backwards in FY2027 despite capex at or above FY2026 levels

  • ~$947M remaining on the share repurchase authorization (untouched in 2026), with buybacks a natural next step as cash generation builds

  • Net leverage 2.2x at end of Q3 2026; cash $3.09B, total debt $3.39B

  • Trading at ~12.7x forward earnings vs. AZO and ORLY at 15x and 24x, and vs. a 20-year average of ~18x

  • ~6x normalized earnings power of close to $7/share

  • 15.8% short interest

  • Share count down ~18.5% over the past 10 years

  • 2.3% dividend yield

Q3 Commentary

Advance’s third quarter was a tale of two halves, with a sluggish start giving way to improving trends and stronger execution across the business. Comp sales declined 1.2%, missing consensus expectations for a 0.4% increase and decelerating from Q2’s -0.5%, while revenue of $2.01B came in ~$30M below the Street. Profitability held up better, with adjusted operating income of $91M ahead of the $88.4M consensus estimate as adjusted operating margins expanded 10 bps Y/Y to 4.5%. Most importantly, management raised its full-year free cash flow guidance by 50% to ~$150M, an improvement of more than $400M Y/Y that will mark Advance’s first full year of positive free cash flow since FY2022.

The weakness in the headline comp was largely a function of where the quarter started. The low point came in the final four weeks of Q2, which ended in mid-July, when comps declined ~3% on a nearly 7% drop in DIY, which management described as the channel’s weakest stretch of the year. From there, trends steadily improved, with comps down ~2% through the first eight weeks of Q3 before turning positive in the final four weeks as DIY declines narrowed to the low single digits. That momentum has carried into Q4, with Pro sales growing at a low-to-mid single-digit rate in the early weeks of the quarter, while management’s full-year comp guidance of ~1% implies further acceleration in overall comps.

That acceleration in Pro continues a trend that has been the steadiest part of the business all year. The channel, which accounts for ~half of sales, grew at a low-single-digit rate in Q3, remained positive every month, and reached ~3% growth in the final four weeks. Main Street Pro, the local two- or three-bay shops that account for ~80% of Pro sales and carry better margins, outpaced the overall channel by ~100 bps, driven by new customer wins and existing accounts moving into higher weekly spending tiers. That is the payoff from better parts availability and consistently getting deliveries out in under 40 minutes.

Keep in mind that reported Pro growth continues to understate the underlying strength, as management deliberately walks away from lower-margin national accounts to concentrate on Main Street. This self-imposed headwind weighed ~100 bps on Pro growth in the quarter (~50 bps on total sales). With that headwind set to roll off by early Q1, reported Pro growth should accelerate in 2027 even before accounting for any further improvement in the business.

DIY, the other half of the business, has been the harder fight. It’s no secret that Advance caters to the lower- and middle-income consumer, and with DIY accounting for ~half of sales, pressure on that customer is hard to miss in the comp. That matters for margins as well as sales, as DIY is Advance’s highest-margin channel, meaning any recovery would bring a mix tailwind alongside it. The channel declined at a low-single-digit rate in Q3, yet nearly every metric tied to O’Kelly’s initiatives continued to move in the right direction. Better training, service, and in-store execution pushed Net Promoter Scores above 80 from the high 70s last quarter, while in-store attachment rates climbed to the mid-30% range from ~30% and DIY units per transaction grew at a low-single-digit rate, driving average ticket growth above same-SKU inflation.

Management is pulling every internal lever available, from the Advance Rewards loyalty program, paid search optimization, and sharper value messaging to the ARGOS private label for customers trading down. Meanwhile, ReliaScan, a free check-engine diagnostic tool, rolled out across most stores during the quarter, and Zebra devices in every store are shifting team member hours from back-room tasks to selling. These encouraging signs tell us that Advance’s internal initiatives are working and translating into better results when customers come through the door. The next step is getting more customers through it.

That is where the macro backdrop is finally starting to turn in Advance’s favor. Much of the pressure on its core customer this year has come down to pain at the pump, with energy accounting for 17.4% of pre-tax income for the bottom 20% of earners, the bulk of which is gasoline, versus just 2.7% for the top quintile.

Gas prices rolled over in late September and have been falling steadily since, dropping ~$0.75 a gallon from the peak to a national average of $3.75, an eight-month low, with RBOB gasoline futures now below $2.50, pointing to more relief ahead.

The spending data responded almost exactly as you would expect. BofA data show lower-income households posted the strongest total card spending growth of any group in October at +5.9%, while holiday spending by lower-income households, which trailed every other cohort in October of both 2024 and 2025, is now up ~9% Y/Y. Broader October retail sales confirmed the strength, rising 6.8% Y/Y for the strongest annual gain since October 2022.

Source: ZeroHedge

Lower gas prices will continue to bring inflation expectations down, which goes hand in hand with consumer sentiment, as seen below:

Less pain at the pump points to a lift in sentiment from today’s washed-out levels, with the UMich index at 48 in October, within a stone’s throw of May’s reading of 44.8. If May does ultimately prove to be the trough, the historical data is encouraging: following the last nine sentiment troughs, the S&P 500 delivered an average 12-month return of 24.1%. The point is, these are the times to be BUYERS of beaten-down consumer names, not SELLERS.

Beyond the consumer backdrop, ~90% of what Advance sells is tied to maintenance and break/fix needs. Q3 strength came from maintenance and failure categories like motor oil, batteries, and wipers, while hard parts remained weak as customers put off larger repairs. But deferred maintenance can only be kicked down the road for so long. The average age of U.S. light vehicles reached a record 12.8 years in 2025 and is expected to hit 13.0 years this year, with more than 110M vehicles now sitting in the prime aftermarket service window of 6 to 14 years. That represents nearly 38% of the fleet, a share S&P Global expects to reach ~40% by 2028.

In the meantime, management continues to control what it can, with the supply chain remaining the centerpiece of that effort. The distribution network has been consolidated from nearly 40 facilities running multiple systems to 15 operating on a single warehouse management platform, with process improvements rolling through each DC in stages through mid-2027 to lower handling costs, improve shipment accuracy, and shorten lead times. Carrier contracts have also been rebid, consolidating volume across 70% fewer carriers for 20+ bps of cost savings, even in a flattish sales environment.

The market hub network, modeled on the hub-and-spoke system that best-in-class peers have used for years, reached 46 locations following 13 openings YTD, with 70%+ of stores set to sit inside a hub ecosystem by year end and ~60 hubs expected to serve the majority of the store base by mid-2027. Each hub carries ~85,000 SKUs for same-day availability, with hub markets historically delivering ~100 bps of comp lift.

These self-help initiatives across the supply chain, merchandising, and stores have already driven significant margin improvement with very little help from the top line. Advance delivered a 4.5% adjusted operating margin in Q3 despite a negative comp, with SG&A dollars down ~2% Y/Y. Management noted that, excluding the tariff refunds received last quarter, it was one of the strongest margin quarters since the strategic plan began two years ago. Zooming out, adjusted operating margins have climbed from a trough of 0.4% in FY2024, the weakest level in more than 20 years, to 2.5% in FY2025 and ~4.15% at the midpoint of FY2026 guidance. That progress has come alongside comp growth of just 0.8% last year and ~1% this year.

For 2027, management continues to expect at least another 100 bps of margin expansion, but guided investors to build off the second half of this year rather than the full year, given ~30 bps of tariff refunds that won’t repeat and fuel and deleveraging pressures likely to linger into the first half. That puts next year’s adjusted operating margin at ~4.7%, driven by merchandising initiatives, labor productivity, and supply chain savings, including 20+ bps from transportation.

More consistent comp growth remains the missing piece of the turnaround and the key to unlocking Advance’s longer-term margin potential. The original roadmap assumed steady low-single-digit comp growth, which has been slow to materialize, pushing out the timeline to management’s still-intact medium-term operating margin target of 7%. The good news is that, with its national account headwind behind it and a stronger Pro business, alongside even a modest recovery in DIY traffic, Advance has what we believe is its strongest top-line setup since the turnaround began.

At a 7% margin on ~$9B of revenue, Advance would generate ~$630M of operating income, a level we believe supports close to $7 per share in normalized earnings power, more than double the current run rate. For context, Advance generated 9% to 11% operating margins before the missteps that derailed the business, while O’Reilly and AutoZone operate at 18% to 20% today, leaving plenty of room to close the gap.

Meanwhile, the importance of the free cash flow inflection can’t be overstated. YTD free cash flow sits at +$109M versus an outflow of $277M last year, with the raised ~$150M full-year target coming even as capex steps up to ~$300M to fund new market hubs, new stores, store upgrades, and in-store technology. Management expects free cash flow to improve again in 2027, even with capex at or above this year’s level. That cash gives Advance the flexibility to keep investing in growth while chipping away at its debt, supporting the goal of returning to investment grade and eventually resuming share buybacks.

While the market has grown impatient waiting for the turnaround to move faster, we believe it underappreciates how much of the foundation has been rebuilt over the past few years and the upside that creates. At just 12.7x forward earnings, the bar is low enough that modest top-line improvement and consistent execution will be enough to move the stock. With much of the heavy lifting behind it and the road ahead starting to clear, Advance looks well positioned for a stronger 2027.
