Q3 Commentary

For a company the market has long treated as a housing proxy, Stanley Black & Decker keeps finding ways to grow without any help from housing. Organic growth accelerated to 4% in Q3 on revenue of $3.73B, landing at the high end of guidance and marking the fastest pace since Q4 2021. Adjusted EPS of $2.31 and adjusted gross margin of 39.4% both benefited from IEEPA tariff refunds, which generated a $180.7M pretax gain in the quarter, worth ~$0.67 of EPS and ~430 bps of margin. Backing out the tariff benefit, the underlying results were every bit as strong. Adjusted EPS of ~$1.64 (+14.7% Y/Y) still topped the ~$1.56 consensus and the high end of guidance, while adjusted gross margin of ~35.1% cleared the long-awaited 35% threshold at the heart of the entire turnaround. That prompted management to raise FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.95-$6.25 (+31% Y/Y at the midpoint) and its free cash flow outlook to $1.0-$1.2B (vs. $688M in FY25), with the underlying operational outlook unchanged.

We laid out the full thesis last month (see article below), walking through how SWK has pulled its own levers to grow and expand margins while housing remains in the gutter.

Little has changed since then. Housing remains under pressure, with management still planning around a flat-to-down tools market, yet SWK continues to take share through its own execution. That progress was well underway before the tariff refunds arrived, but the refunds have given the strategy a shot in the arm. Rather than let them flow straight to the bottom line, management is directing the bulk toward growth investments on top of the $75-100M already planned for 2026. In effect, it is pulling forward $70-80M of spending originally earmarked for 2027 to expand its field presence, step up digital marketing and brand activation, while accelerating new product innovation.

Those investments continue to gain traction, with organic growth climbing from flat in Q1 to +3% in Q2 and +4% in Q3. That puts FY26 on track to be SWK’s first year of positive organic growth since the pandemic-driven pull-forward in 2021.

Power tools once again did the heavy lifting in Q3, accelerating to +10% organic growth from +8% in Q2, which had already marked the category’s strongest growth in several years. Much of that strength traces back to the pro customer. The U.S. commercial and industrial channel accelerated to mid-teens growth from low double digits last quarter as data center construction and a broad backlog of other job site work keep pro demand running hot, a trend management expects to continue. U.S. retail added mid-single-digit growth of its own, a solid result given how long the DIY customer has been under pressure.

Most encouraging is how broad the growth has become. For years, DEWALT was left to carry the portfolio on its own, but STANLEY and CRAFTSMAN have now joined it, with all three brands delivering organic growth for two consecutive quarters. That consistency is a direct result of one of the biggest changes under CEO Chris Nelson, who reorganized the company around its brands rather than individual product lines, giving each its own general manager and a clearly defined end user.

Built for the pro, DEWALT grew across every region as investments in end-user specialists embedded with each trade continue to pay off. Those efforts are pulling more pros into a battery ecosystem where more than 80% of users stick with the same platform on their next purchase. CRAFTSMAN, repositioned as SWK’s DIY brand, is in its most active launch year since being acquired in 2017. Influencer partnerships are driving record brand engagement, while a ~30% reduction in new product development time across the company, with platforming serving as a major productivity unlock, is helping bring new tools to market faster. STANLEY, which generates more than 60% of its sales in Europe, is working through an eight-wave refresh of its product lines, now supported by a dedicated sales force focused on the European hand tool wholesalers that drive the business.

Management expects that momentum to carry into the fourth quarter, guiding to +3-4% organic growth in Tools & Outdoor and keeping the segment on track for low-single-digit organic growth for the full year.

Home Depot and Lowe’s both reported results this week for quarters that ran about a month past SWK’s quarter-end, offering a positive early read on Q4. Home Depot (15% of sales) beat expectations with its highest comp growth in four years, led by double-digit comps in its power tools department, while its Pro customer continued to outpace DIY. Lowe’s (12% of sales) also beat, with comps up 1.8% on positive growth in tools and hardware. It also cited strong Pro demand for new DEWALT generators and an expanded lineup that now gives it the largest DEWALT assortment of any U.S. home improvement retailer. Both retailers raised full-year sales guidance on steady underlying demand, with SWK’s brands front and center heading into the key holiday selling season.

The progress on adjusted gross margin has been just as impressive. Excluding refunds, adjusted gross margin of ~35.1% expanded 350 bps Y/Y on productivity and favorable mix, up from ~31.2% in Q2 and more than 15 ppts above the 19.5% trough in Q4 2022. Including refunds, YTD adjusted gross margin now stands at 34.4% (+460 bps Y/Y), keeping FY26 on track for ~34.2% (~350 bps of expansion, ~150 bps from refunds).

Even as that refund benefit falls away, management expects to land at or very close to 35% in 2027, with another 150-200 bps of net productivity gains and a modest low-single-digit price increase offsetting rising inflation. That keeps the long-awaited 35-37% target for 2028 firmly in place. For context, the last time SWK cleared 35% for a full year was 2018, when it earned $8.15 per share and the stock traded north of $150. With a far leaner cost structure today and a shrinking share count, we see a path not only back to those earnings levels, but considerably beyond over time.

That margin progress is translating just as clearly into free cash flow. Q3 free cash flow of $585M came in well ahead of the ~$222M the Street was expecting, bringing YTD free cash flow to $836M versus an outflow of $195M a year ago. At the $1.1B midpoint of FY26 guidance, backing out ~$300M of tariff refunds and adding back ~$200M of one-time taxes and fees tied to the CAM sale leaves ~$1.0B of underlying free cash flow, or a ~6.2% yield at today’s price.

With leverage heading toward ~2.5x by year-end and balance sheet repair now a closed chapter, that cash is making its way back to shareholders. SWK repurchased $500M of stock this year, retiring ~4% of its shares, before the Board approved a new $1B authorization in October. That comes alongside a ~3.0% dividend yield and a payout history spanning 150 consecutive years, with 59 straight annual increases, the longest such record of any industrial company on the NYSE.

With the stock up 54% YTD and more than double its lows, the market has clearly started to reward SWK for its execution. Shares now trade at ~17x forward earnings, in line with their historical average, so a breather after such a big move would come as no surprise. Zooming out, however, we still see this story in its early innings. Execution alone has carried the stock this far, with the housing tailwind still ahead. A ~4M-unit housing shortage, an average home now ~42 years old, and millennials moving into their prime family formation years all point to a recovery being a matter of when, not if. From today’s depressed levels, we continue to see the risk-reward in housing as firmly skewed to the upside. When housing finally turns, it will be the whipped cream and cherry on top of an already improving business.

Q3 Earnings Breakdown

10 Key Points

1) SWK reported Q3 revenue of $3.73B, down 0.6% Y/Y on a reported basis and up 4% organically. The figure was in line with consensus and at the top end of the 3% to 4% organic growth guide. Higher volume (+6%) was offset by lower pricing (-2%) and a ~4% portfolio drag from the CAM divestiture and the transition to a licensing model for gas walk-behind outdoor products, with currency flat. Organic growth accelerated from flat in Q1 and +3% in Q2 to its highest quarterly level since 2021. Volume strength was concentrated in U.S. retail (up mid-single digits) and the commercial and industrial (C&I) channel (up mid-teens) within Tools & Outdoor. YTD revenue reached $11.54B (+0.8% Y/Y), with YTD organic growth of ~2%.

2) Adjusted EPS of $2.31 came in well ahead of consensus of ~$1.56 and $0.76 above the midpoint of July guidance, up 61.5% Y/Y from $1.43. The outperformance was driven primarily by net tariff refunds (~$0.67 after related incentive compensation, growth investments, and taxes), along with ~$0.02 each from a lower share count and lower net interest expense. Excluding refunds, adjusted EPS of ~$1.64 (+14.7% Y/Y) still cleared both consensus and the high end of the $1.50 to $1.60 guide. YTD adjusted EPS reached $4.66 versus $3.26 last year (+42.9%).

3) Adjusted gross margin reached 39.4% in Q3, up 780 bps Y/Y, with ~430 bps coming from net tariff refunds. Even excluding refunds, adjusted gross margin of ~35.1% (+350 bps Y/Y) topped consensus of ~34.3%, clearing the 35% threshold on net productivity gains and favorable product mix. That compares to ~31.2% ex-refunds in Q2, bringing YTD adjusted gross margin to 34.4% (+460 bps Y/Y). For the full year, management now expects ~350 bps of expansion off FY25’s 30.7%, including ~150 bps from net tariff refunds. Q4 remains guided to 34% to 35% (vs. 33.3% last year) on continued productivity and tariff mitigation initiatives, with the long-term target of above 35% toward 37% unchanged.

4) The Tools & Outdoor segment posted Q3 net sales of $3.34B, up 2% on a reported basis and 4% organically. Higher volume (+7%) was partially offset by lower pricing (-3%) and a 2% drag from the gas walk-behind licensing transition, with currency flat. Management noted that lower pricing reflects the promotional calendar reset running to plan, with list prices holding. Growth was led by power tools, where organic growth accelerated to +10% from +8% in Q2, alongside a 2% gain in hand tools, accessories, and storage, partially offset by a 12% decline in Outdoor on weather pressure. North America grew 6% organically on U.S. retail up mid-single digits and C&I up mid-teens. Europe grew 1%, while Rest of World declined 1% on softer Latin America, bringing YTD segment organic growth to ~2%. Adjusted segment margin of 17.6% expanded 560 bps Y/Y, with ~430 bps from net tariff refunds and the balance from net productivity and favorable mix. Management still expects low-single-digit organic growth for the segment in FY26, driven by share gains in a ~flat to down market.

5) The Engineered Fastening segment (~11% of total sales) posted Q3 net sales of $396M, down 21% on a reported basis but up 2% organically. The CAM divestiture created a 22% headwind, partially offset by volume (+1%) and pricing (+1%), with currency down 1%. Industrial grew 10% organically on project-driven wins and solid commercial execution, more than offsetting a 2% decline in Automotive as OEM customers grew more cautious on launches, production schedules, and capital deployment. Adjusted segment margin of 11.7% declined 110 bps Y/Y on automotive demand pressure, with the segment receiving no tariff refund benefit. YTD segment organic growth stands at ~4%, helped by aerospace strength in Q1 before the CAM sale. Given the deterioration in auto, management lowered its FY26 outlook to low-single-digit organic growth (from low-to-mid single digits), with a flat Y/Y segment margin (previously positive).

6) Cash from operating activities of $659M drove free cash flow of $585M in the quarter, up 276.7% from $155M last year and well ahead of consensus of ~$222M. Performance was supported by both operational cash generation and net tariff refunds, alongside disciplined working capital management, with inventories down to $3.84B from $4.16B at year-end. YTD free cash flow reached $836M versus an outflow of $195M a year ago, already well above FY25’s $688M. Management raised FY26 FCF guidance by $400M at the midpoint to $1.0B to $1.2B (from $600M to $800M), versus consensus of ~$775M. The new range incorporates YTD outperformance and refunds received, net of projected CAM-related taxes and fees.

7) SWK repurchased ~2.5M shares for $250M in Q3, fully utilizing the $500M authorization approved in April (~5.8M shares repurchased in total), with diluted share count down 2.2% Y/Y to ~148.6M. The Board followed with a new $1B repurchase authorization on October 29, running through October 2029. With management describing the company as being at the end of its major transformational cycle and any future portfolio moves limited to pruning around the edges, capital allocation priorities now center on funding organic growth, returning capital to shareholders, and bolt-on M&A when appropriate. On the dividend front, the quarterly payout stands at $0.84 per share (~3% yield), extending a record of 150 consecutive years of payments, alongside 59 consecutive years of increases.

8) SWK ended Q3 with $741M of cash (up from $280M at year-end) against $4.7B of long-term debt, with short-term borrowings fully paid down from $606M at year-end. Total liquidity stands at ~$3.7B, with no debt maturities until 2028. The lower debt load and strong YTD cash generation have also brought the full-year net interest expense estimate down to ~$250M from ~$255M. Management remains on track for net debt to adjusted EBITDA of ~2.5x by year-end, inclusive of buybacks, down from 5.9x at the end of 2023, with maintaining an investment-grade credit rating a stated priority.

9) SWK has now received the vast majority of the IEEPA tariff refunds it applied for, recognizing a $180.7M pretax gain in Q3 ($298.7M YTD), with FY26 adjusted EPS guidance including ~$0.60 of net refund benefit. Rather than letting the refunds fall to the bottom line, management is using them to pull forward $70M to $80M of growth investment originally planned for 2027 across field presence, brand activation, and the new product pipeline. That lifts FY26 SG&A to ~23.5% to 24% of sales (including ~80 bps of refund-related costs) before returning toward ~23% in 2027. On the cost side, the temporary period of lower tariffs since late February is still largely offsetting rising inflation in steel, electrical components, resins, battery metals, and tungsten, with tariffs assumed to return to IEEPA levels very late in the year. With inflation to address in 2027 regardless of the tariff path, management plans to pair continued productivity with a price increase likely around the turn of the year.

10) SWK raised and tightened FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.95 to $6.25 from a prior range of $5.20 to $5.80, with the $6.10 midpoint implying +31% Y/Y growth versus consensus of ~$5.60. Of the $0.60 midpoint increase, ~$0.55 reflects incremental Q3 net tariff refunds. The remaining ~$0.05 comes from a lower share count (~150M from ~151M) and below-the-line items, leaving the underlying operational outlook unchanged and excluding any potential Q4 refunds. Total revenue is still expected to be ~flat Y/Y, with low-single-digit organic growth driven by solid volume and ~flat pricing. For Q4, management guided to net sales of ~$3.6B, organic growth of 2% to 4%, and adjusted EPS of ~$1.45, including ~$0.25 of incremental costs and taxes tied to refunds already received.

data.title: Nvidia Doubled Revenue. P/E Fell To A 10-Year Low
data.description:
"Our momentum is real," Colette Kress said on 17 November, in her first results release as Nvidia's (NVDA) interim CEO. The figures backed her up. Revenue more than doubled in a year, to $115.8 billion, and the forecast for the current quarter came in above what analysts expected. The next day the shares fell 2.9%.

That is Nvidia's puzzle right now. The company earns more every quarter, and the market pays less for each dollar of it. At the 18 November close Nvidia traded at its lowest multiple of earnings in at least ten years. The report itself explains a good part of why.

Rubin's record start

In the three months to 25 October, Nvidia sold nearly twice as much as in all of fiscal 2024. Data center sales, the chips, networking and systems that train and run AI models, came to $107.6 billion of it, up 110%.

Much of the jump came from Vera Rubin, the rack-scale system that began shipping in the quarter. Kress told analysts it brought in nearly $20 billion in its first quarter, the fastest ramp in Nvidia's history. Networking, the gear that links thousands of chips into one machine, passed $21 billion.

The rest of Nvidia, now reported as Edge Computing, grew 42% to $8.2 billion on workstations and chips for robots and cars, while higher memory prices weighed on gaming PCs.

Nvidia revenue by customer

Nvidia splits its data center sales by customer, and the split tells a new story. Sales to hyperscale customers, the giant cloud and internet platforms, rose 71% to $60.1 billion. Sales to everyone else, a group of AI clouds, industrial companies and enterprises, nearly tripled to $47.5 billion.

A year ago that second group was under a third of data center sales. Now it is 44%. A longer customer list spreads Nvidia's risk, and it also brings in buyers with far less cash of their own than Microsoft or Amazon, the AI cloud start-ups above all.

How the buildout gets paid for

Those newer buyers need money, and Nvidia increasingly provides the backing. Its $32 billion of agreements with neoclouds, the young AI cloud companies, depend on those partners raising financing. It has also agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion of credit support for SB Energy's campus in Ohio, which will host Nvidia systems under 20-year leases to OpenAI.

Customers are paying more slowly, too. Money owed to Nvidia for chips already delivered rose to $81 billion, and the average customer now takes 64 days to pay, up from 60 a quarter earlier. Nvidia puts part of that down to longer payment terms on large multi-quarter deals with some investment-grade customers.

The cash still pours in. Free cash flow nearly doubled, and Nvidia returned a record $28.1 billion to shareholders, $22.1 billion of it through buybacks.

Nvidia's biggest customers already lean on borrowing, as we wrote in Nvidia's Biggest Customers Keep Spending. Power and Debt Set the Limits. Now the supplier stands behind part of the bill as well.

Why Nvidia stock fell after earnings

Then the price went the other way. Nvidia's earnings per share over the last four quarters rose 130% on a year earlier. Over the same year the share price fell 17%, and at the 18 November close it sat 37% below its record on 6 October.

Put those two together and the multiple collapses. Nvidia traded at 16x its trailing earnings, below every month-end reading of the past ten years. The low before this was 18x, in December 2018, and the ten-year median is 54x.

Two things explain much of the latest drop. The first sits at the top. Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and ran it from the start, resigned as CEO on 12 November, and the filing gave no reason. Kress runs the company until the board names a successor, Harvey Jones became its first chair, and an independent board committee is still investigating. On the earnings call the board ruled out bringing Huang back. From the last close before the news, the shares lost 13%.

The second is the forecast. The quarter to January has an extra week, so per week $130 billion is only about 4% above this quarter's pace, by our arithmetic, after 20% growth from the quarter before.

The forecast excludes data center compute revenue from China, compared with $2.4 billion of shipments there this quarter, and gross margin is guided down to 71% to 72% as Rubin ramps. Kress still expects revenue to grow about 75% next fiscal year.

How much Nvidia is in the S&P 500 and other ETFs

Most investors own Nvidia through a fund, and how much they own depends on which one. It is about 6% of both SPY, the S&P 500 fund, and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund. Growth and tech funds hold more: about 10% of VUG, Vanguard's growth fund, and 14% of VGT, its tech fund.

Of these funds, the biggest share sits in SMH, VanEck's chip fund, at 17%. SOXX, the iShares chip fund, holds about 7%, because its index caps the weight of its largest companies.

That share is the lever. With everything else unchanged, a 10% move in Nvidia moves SPY by about 0.6% and SMH by about 1.7%.

The P/E here is the share price over the last four quarters of reported earnings per share; the fund shares are our look-through of each fund's holdings at the 18 November close.

Kress called the momentum real, and the report agrees. What the market will pay for it has not been this low in ten years.

data.title: Scotia Metals’ Lithium Ambition: The Mine Builders Behind a New Exploration Story
data.description:
Dallas, United States, November 19th, 2026, FinanceWire


Disseminated on behalf of the issuer; Scotia Metals Corp.

After helping advance lithium operations and companies that became part of multibillion-dollar transactions, Scotia’s leadership is now pursuing two early-stage discovery opportunities as industry forecasts point to an urgent need for new supply.

Scotia Metals Corp. (CSE: SMET) (OTCQB: CSRVF) (FSE: C6R0) has secured an option to acquire the Nordestina lithium project in Bahia, Brazil, while advancing its inaugural drilling campaign at Acadia in Nova Scotia. But the broader reason Scotia could attract attention is the identity of the people building the Company: executives whose careers include major lithium mine developments, financings and resource specific mergers and acquisitions.

For early-stage exploration companies, drilling and assays determine geological prospects. Yet the ability to recognize opportunities, evaluate technical results, secure capital and eventually execute a project is also consequential. Scotia’s leadership has worked across several important chapters of the hard-rock lithium industry. Now it is building a new project portfolio before either Scotia property has established a mineral resource.

The Management Connection: Experience Built at Scale

Chairman Brian Talbot has more than 25 years of lithium operating and development experience, according to Scotia’s corporate profile. He held senior operating responsibilities at Galaxy Resources, including work at the Mt Cattlin operation in Australia, and served as chief operating officer of Sigma Lithium (Nasdaq: SGML) (TSX-V: SGML), overseeing commissioning of the Grota do Cirilo operation in Brazil. Scotia reports that Sigma reached approximately US$4.8 billion in market capitalization during his tenure. That is a historical valuation of Sigma, not a return earned by Scotia shareholders.

Director Nick Rowley was Galaxy’s director of corporate development and played a role in its merger with Orocobre, which created Allkem. Allkem later combined with Livent to form Arcadium Lithium, acquired by Rio Tinto (NYSE: RIO) in 2025 for approximately US$6.7 billion. Rowley also has experience with lithium project financing and offtake arrangements through RTEK International. These transactions illustrate the scale of businesses with which Scotia directors have been associated, not value created solely by any one individual.

CEO Rodrigo Roso brings roughly two decades of legal, M&A and project-development experience, including work involving Sigma Lithium and other mining businesses. Scotia director Shawn Khunkhun previously led Dolly Varden Silver which merged with Contango ORE, Inc. to create Contango Silver & Gold Inc. (NYSE: CTGO), a North American mid-tier precious metals producer and developer. Together, the team gives the company experience spanning exploration-stage strategy, operations, corporate development and capital markets.

The intriguing question is whether that experience can help Scotia efficiently identify and advance an economic lithium asset. The answer will depend on exploration results, financing, permitting and many other factors. Prior success at different companies does not predict a comparable outcome at Scotia.

Nordestina: Expanding Scotia’s Search Into Brazil

The Nordestina option adds a 16,566-hectare property comprising nine mineral permits in northeastern Bahia, Brazil, alongside Scotia’s Canadian flagship. Field crews have visually identified suspected spodumene at roughly 100 locations over an approximately 3.3-kilometer corridor. A total of 1,355 rock and soil samples were submitted for laboratory analysis, with initial assays anticipated in late November under the company’s stated schedule. Visual observations are preliminary and do not establish lithium grade, tonnage or an economic deposit.

The agreement allows Scotia to evaluate the property before committing the full acquisition price. It calls for US$10,000 monthly payments and reimbursement of up to US$210,000 in prior RTEK exploration expenses, with a US$2 million purchase price payable only upon exercise. Scotia has no minimum exploration spending requirement, can terminate on 30 days’ notice, and has until May 31, 2028 to exercise. This flexible structure may be especially relevant to an exploration-stage company deciding how to allocate capital across multiple targets.

Acadia: A Drilling Catalyst Already Underway

At Acadia, Scotia began a six-hole program of approximately 1,000 meters on November 9, targeting a possible bedrock source of spodumene-bearing boulder trains. The Company has documented five boulder trains spread across roughly 3 by 1 kilometers. Historical selected samples have graded up to 3.40% lithium oxide (Li₂O), and 20 of 38 channel samples from the recent program exceeded 1.0% Li₂O. These are surface and selected sample results, not drill intersections or an established resource.

The next meaningful step is to establish what, if anything, lies in bedrock beneath or near these surface indicators. Favorable results could guide additional work and raise the technical significance of the project; unsuccessful holes would require the exploration thesis to be reassessed. Full results were expected during the first quarter of 2027 under Scotia’s previously announced timeline.

The Supply Challenge: 134 New Mines and More Than US$100 Billion

The strategic backdrop is substantial. In October 2026, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence projected global lithium demand of approximately 7 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) annually by 2050, versus 2.11 million tonnes in 2026. Under its assumptions, that incremental demand is equivalent to production from 134 new lithium mines averaging 36,000 tonnes LCE per year. Expressed another way, the world would need to add the equivalent of a new mine about every two months for 24 years, requiring more than US$100 billion of investment. Benchmark’s upside-demand scenario points to more than 180 equivalent new mines.

The International Energy Agency’s 2026 outlook separately projects lithium demand to quadruple by 2040 and mined output to increase approximately 2.5-fold. Its assessment also indicates that anticipated projects may leave lithium supply deficits through 2035. These are scenario-based forecasts rather than guaranteed shortages; recycling, new technology, commodity prices and policy can materially change the outcome.

This creates an industry-wide tension: forecast demand may be enormous, but discovering a deposit is only the first stage. Successful new mines require teams capable of technical assessment, financing, permitting, construction, commissioning and commercialization. That is why Scotia’s management history is a relevant part of its story, even before any resource has been defined.

Why Scotia Deserves a Place on the Exploration Watchlist

Scotia’s case rests on a combination of management experience and identifiable upcoming technical events, not on a claim that a mine already exists. Nordestina offers a new potential target with pending laboratory data and limited immediate acquisition commitments. Acadia offers a drilling program intended to test the source of compelling but still preliminary surface indicators. If exploration delivers positive evidence, Scotia could have more information with which to plan follow-up programs and assess future development pathways.

A leadership team with experience at Galaxy, Sigma and other lithium businesses gives the opportunity a distinctive dimension: the people assessing Scotia’s early-stage properties have participated in building and advancing far more mature operations. Whether they can replicate any element of that trajectory here remains uncertain. For investors following the long-term supply buildout in lithium, the combination of experienced operators and near-term exploration results makes Scotia a company to monitor closely, with the risks inherent in junior mineral exploration fully in view.

data.title: Questions About Fed Rate Hikes Nobody Is Asking
data.description:
Gold and silver took it on the chin again on Wednesday. Gold fell below $3,750, and silver crashed through $46.

Why?

Fed people said some stuff.

The Federal Reserve released the minutes from the October meeting on Wednesday. Unsurprisingly, it reflected significant hawkishness among the committee members.

The minutes described inflation pressure as “broad-based,” and the committee essentially promised future rate hikes.

“Almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective.”

During an interview aired by CNBC, Fed governor Christopher Waller doubled down on the hawkish talk. Apparently, he doesn’t share Kevin Warsh’s aversion to “forward guidance.”

Waller said inflation is “heading in the wrong direction and is spreading out,” emphasizing that we can't blame every rising price on the oil shock. He insisted, "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking aggressive actions," hinting at a 50-basis-point rate hike in December.

So, there ya go! Rate hikes are locked in. Sell your gold and silver. Interest rates will remain higher for longer.

Will they, though?

Tunnel Vision

Before examining the assumptions more deeply, I have a more fundamental question.

Are we obsessing too much about what the Federal Reserve might do without thinking through all the possible ramifications?

The markets seem to have tunnel vision right now. All they can see is “the Fed hiking rates” and “interest rates higher for longer.”

News Gold Letter publisher Brien Lundin said the markets seem to have developed an “obsession” with Federal Reserve monetary policy.

“While it has always been an important factor in market analysis, it has grown to be the all-important consideration ever since the Great Financial Crisis. Like suckling piglets fighting for access to their mother’s milk, traders have been blinded to anything else in their investment decisions.”

He also pointed out that their addiction to easy money has made the markets “tolerant to the drug of monetary adrenaline, while also heightening their response to any indication of potentially hawkish policies.”

Lundin thinks this obsession has caused a bad case of tunnel vision, and mainstream market analysts are missing the big picture as they fixate on interest rates.

“What both the Fed and traders are ignoring, of course, are the long-term implications of higher interest rates.”

In other words, policies have consequences, and they aren’t always the ones you hope for or expect.

The Questions Nobody’s Asking

Everybody just assumes the Fed will hike rates and then hold them higher until inflation comes down. They also assume that it will work.

That’s debatable.

In the first place, what makes people think a modest 25-basis-point rate hike will slay inflation that has been above the 2 percent target for 68 months? Do you remember how much easy money central banks and governments created during the pandemic? Do you remember money creation during the Great Recession?

When the Fed launched quantitative easing (QE) in 2008, Ben Bernanke insisted it was a “temporary” emergency measure. He swore the Fed would only hold those bonds on its balance sheet for a short time. He promised that the Fed wasn’t monetizing the debt.

Nearly 20 years later, the balance sheet is multiple times larger than when Ben made his promise.

When Paul Volcker tackled inflation in 1980, he quickly jacked rates up to 20 percent. I’m not suggesting the Fed would need to hike that high to drive down the current wave of inflation. However, it’s fair to question whether 5 or 6 percent interest rates are adequate for the job.

In that sense, I agree with the central bankers' rhetoric. Inflation is high. Inflation is persistent. The central bank needs to act.

Which kind of makes you wonder: why haven’t they done more? It’s not like the central bankers haven’t had time. It’s been over five and a half years since CPI was at 2 percent.

And why is the Fed running inflationary QE operations right now, even as the committee members fret about too much inflation?

I’ll tell you why.

The massive debt black hole.

Mainstream analysis tends to avoid this issue like a stinky dog. They just tell us, “The Fed will hike!” and move along without considering what might happen when it does. I guess they assume that inflation will come down and the economy will march merrily along.

They might be right.

But they probably aren’t.

Economies buried in debt and addicted to easy money don’t fare well in a higher-interest-rate environment. The Fed people won’t say it out loud, but they know it’s true. They must be aware that if they keep hiking, they will collapse the debt-riddled bubble economy.

As already noted, most of that inflation generated during the Great Recession and the pandemic remains in the system.  The malinvestments and resource misallocations inherent in easy-money eras were never cleaned out. We’ve enjoyed an easy money boom for nearly two decades. Do you know what comes after a boom?

A bust.

We’re due.

Rate hikes may well be the pin that finally pops the bubble.  

You might want to think this through before you dump your gold and silver just because “rates are going up.”

data.title: The U.S. Treasury’s Short-Term Debt Gamble
data.description:
U.S. Treasury issuance in 2026 has had a weighted average maturity of just 1.7 years, compared with 9.8 years for U.S. corporate bonds. This contrast highlights two very different financing strategies. Corporate America is increasingly relying on longer-term debt to fund investments in AI infrastructure, data centers, and technology systems, which require substantial upfront capital and years to generate returns. Meanwhile, the Treasury is leaning toward shorter-term financing, potentially limiting borrowing costs in today's high-interest-rate environment while betting that it will be able to refinance at lower rates within the next two years. This strategy, however, exposes the government to greater refinancing risk if interest rates remain elevated.

data.title: Silver Investors Should Watch The Vaults, Not Just The Price
data.description:
Silver has slipped below $45 an ounce, yet the big vaults in London and New York have not been filling up, which means the fall is not coming from a surplus of metal, and the supply case for owning silver still stands.

If silver were piling up unsold, the big warehouses would usually show it. They do not. London held less silver at the end of October than a month earlier, the first fall in six months. In New York, the metal ready for delivery against futures barely moved while the price dropped. And India, the world's biggest silver consumer, spent nearly three times as much on silver imports in October as in September. On the stockpiles alone, that is a small positive for silver holders, based on one month of data. It is not a sign of a squeeze, and the next test starts on November 30.

Silver traded near $44.93 an ounce late on November 18. It was down about 5% on the day. Hawkish minutes from the Federal Reserve's last meeting added to bets on a December rate rise. The gold-silver ratio stood near 83, meaning one ounce of gold buys about 83 ounces of silver. Silver is now about 37% below its 2025 close. The latest premium issue at Golden Meadow® found the inventory picture calmer than the price.

There are six Deep Dives in this issue of the premium Silver Catalyst newsletter, and in this article, I'll focus on one of them.

 

London: The First Fall in Six Months

London is the centre of the world's wholesale silver trade, where large bars are stored. At the end of October its vaults held 28,889 tonnes, about 928.8 million ounces (Moz), according to the LBMA's monthly data. That is about 3.1 Moz less than at the end of September, after five monthly rises in a row.

A fall in London's stock is a change in where silver sits, not a measure of silver used up. Some of it may have gone to India, some to exchange-traded funds, which hold silver for investors and trade like shares, and some elsewhere. The LBMA does not say.

The vaults are well stocked but not full. They hold about 21% less than at their June 2021 peak. Metals Focus, a research firm, put the metal available outside those funds at about 267 Moz. Kitco reported the estimate alongside end-September vault data. That is nearly double the 136 Moz of London stock outside funds at the end of September 2025. Metals Focus and the Silver Institute called that a "record (reported) low", and it came weeks before London's October squeeze, when buyers struggled to find metal there. The two figures come from different reports and may not cover exactly the same metal. The 267 Moz figure also predates October's data, so the two cannot be combined to work out a new balance.

Funds may also have drawn on that metal. The iShares Silver Trust, which keeps most of its metal in London, added about 11 Moz from the end of September to November 10. If that metal came out of London's stock, the silver not held by funds fell by more than London's reported total did. That is my inference, because the LBMA does not split its figures by owner.

New York: Steady Through the Sell-Off

COMEX is the main US futures exchange, where traders agree a price today for silver delivered later. Its "registered" silver is metal with a warrant, a receipt that makes it ready for delivery. Registered stock stood at 101.63 Moz on November 9, on the exchange's own report. On November 18 it was about 101.2 Moz, on CME Group figures compiled by MetalCharts. The price fell hard over those nine days, and the deliverable metal hardly changed.

Open interest is the number of futures contracts still open. Counted in ounces, it came to about 5.7 for each registered ounce, the same ratio as a week earlier. Money managers, mostly hedge funds, held net bullish bets of 3,615 contracts on November 10. That is their bets on a rise minus their bets on a fall, and it is close to their lowest since February 2024.

So far fewer of these traders are betting on a rise than earlier in the year. The figure does not show how much forced selling is left, though. Large bets in both directions sit inside that small net number and cancel each other out.

Sources: LBMA, October and September 2026 vault data | LBMA, June 2021 record | CME Group, COMEX silver stocks, November 9 | MetalCharts, COMEX silver stocks from CME Group data, November 18 | CFTC, COMEX silver open interest and managed money, November 3 and 10 | Kitco, Metals Focus on London and positioning, October 29 | KNN India, citing Reuters, October 23 | India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry, September and October trade data, via Kitco and The Pamphlet | World Silver Survey 2026, Metals Focus and the Silver Institute

The open-interest ratio pairs the CFTC's November 10 figure with registered stock on November 18. The Kitco report carrying the 267 Moz figure does not give its date; it appears beside end-September vault data. The managed-money figures are longs minus shorts in the CFTC's disaggregated report. India's monthly trade release gives values, not tonnes.

 

India: The Buyer Came Back

India is the world's biggest silver consumer and imports most of what it uses. Dealers told Reuters that in late October the government issued permits to import about 6,500 tonnes over six months. That is about 209 Moz. It comes to roughly nine-tenths of India's imports in all of 2025, which Metals Focus and the Silver Institute put at 232.2 Moz.

A permit is a ceiling, not an order. When the permits were issued, Indian buyers were paying only 45 cents an ounce over official domestic prices. That points to a market that was not short of metal that week.

The first trade figures since then are firmer. India's commerce ministry put October silver imports at $1.91 billion. That is nearly three times September's figure. These are values, not volumes, and the price moved between the two months. October was still about 28% below October 2025, when India was buying heavily during the squeeze in London. November's figures, due in mid-December, will be the first full month under the new permits.

 

What This Means to Silver Investors

The stockpiles tell a different story from the price. A price that falls because there is too much silver around tends to leave metal sitting in vaults. In October, London's stock fell and India's imports rose. Into mid-November, New York's deliverable stock held. On one month of data, that is a small positive for the case that the world uses more silver than it produces.

It is not evidence of a shortage you can see yet. London is well stocked, nothing in New York showed strain, and India's buying came after months of curbs. Market reports blame the price fall largely on expectations of a December rate rise and a firmer dollar.

In their interim review on November 12, Metals Focus and the Silver Institute still forecast a sixth annual shortfall in a row, of about 35 Moz. That is smaller than the 46.3 Moz they expected in April. They also said that fund selling and the smaller shortfall have helped ease tightness this year in the physical market, where bars and coins change hands.

The next tests come quickly. November 30 is the first day buyers holding December contracts can be told their metal is ready for delivery. December is one of COMEX's main delivery months. A smooth month with registered stock near 100 Moz would confirm the calm. The LBMA's November figures follow around December 7, and India's November imports in mid-December. Stockpiles are one of the forces I follow in Silver Rising, and I keep track of how silver has traded against them.

data.title: Bitcoin ETFs Lose $975M In A Week As Russia Moves To Open Bitcoin To Funds
data.description:
S spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) lost a net 4,658 BTC, about $296.7 million, in their latest daily update, on-chain tracker Lookonchain reported on Thursday, November 19. Over seven days, the funds shed 15,314 BTC, or $975.5 million. All five of the largest funds posted outflows on both the day and the week.

On the same day, Russia moved the other way. A Bank of Russia official said the central bank plans rule changes that would let investment funds for qualified investors buy Bitcoin directly, with the first products possible in 2027. Retail access to crypto futures is also being weighed, but later.

We compared the week’s ETF selling with the new coins miners produced over the same days. The selling was almost five times larger. So, can new buyers like Russia fill a gap this big?

Bitcoin ETFs: Every Major Fund Saw Outflows This Week

Lookonchain’s table shows the selling was broad, not limited to one issuer:

  • BlackRock (IBIT): -2,377 BTC on the day and -9,417 BTC over the week, about 61% of the weekly total. It still holds 778,966 BTC, the largest stash by far.

  • Fidelity (FBTC): -1,109 BTC on the day and -2,348 BTC over the week.

  • Grayscale (GBTC and BTC): -265 BTC on the day and -1,455 BTC over the week.

  • Bitwise (BITB) and ARK 21Shares (ARKB): -586 and -308 BTC on the day, -955 and -838 BTC over the week.

Together, the US funds now hold 1,231,539 BTC, worth about $78.45 billion. The week’s outflows equal about 1.2% of that.

Ethereum ETFs saw the same pattern on a smaller scale. They lost 9,904 ETH, about $17.9 million, on the day. Over the week, outflows reached 65,373 ETH, or $117.8 million. BlackRock’s ETHA accounted for most of it.

US BTC ETF Selling Was 4.8 Times the New Supply

Every day, miners create new BTC as a reward for adding blocks to the network. We counted the blocks added in the seven days to Thursday afternoon UTC on mempool.space, a public block explorer: 1,030 blocks at 3.125 BTC each, or about 3,219 new BTC.

  • The gap: ETF outflows of 15,314 BTC were 4.8 times the BTC miners produced in the same week.

  • What it means: when investors pull money from an ETF, the fund gives up coins to pay them back, and most of it ends up sold in the market. Other buyers have to absorb that on top of what miners sell.

  • The price: BTC fell from about $74,000 on November 11 to a low near $62,000 on November 15. It trades near $64,000 now.

This is where Russia’s plan looks small for now. From November 17, ordinary Russian investors can buy BTC through licensed brokers and exchanges, but only up to 300,000 rubles a year per intermediary. That’s about $3,670, or roughly 0.057 BTC at today’s price. It would take about 267,000 Russians buying the full amount to match one week of US ETF selling.

Russia’s Bitcoin Plan: Funds First, Retail Futures Later

Russia legalized regulated crypto trading this year, and the rules are rolling out in steps:

  • Retail spot access: since November 17, retail investors can buy BTC, ETH and USDT after passing a knowledge test. The rules come from a Bank of Russia ordinance that sets the 300,000-ruble yearly cap. Qualified investors, who meet wealth or experience thresholds, have no cap.

  • Qualified funds: Olga Shishlyannikova, who heads the central bank’s department for investment intermediaries, spoke on November 18. She said the bank is considering rule changes next year to let funds for qualified investors buy crypto. Today, those funds can only use derivatives that pay out in cash. The first products could come in 2027, once the changes are registered with the Ministry of Justice.

  • Retail funds and futures: funds for ordinary investors are not part of the plan for now, and retail access to crypto futures is only being weighed, with no timeline.

  • Next steps: Moscow Exchange plans to start crypto trading on December 1, and direct peer-to-peer crypto trades are set to end in July 2027.

For Bitcoin, Russia is a long-term story. Regulated funds could add steady demand from 2027, but none of it arrives in time to offset this month’s ETF selling.

Bitcoin Price Analysis: $62,300 Has Held Twice

On the daily chart, Bitcoin trades at $64,037. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $75,258, and its 200-day EMA at $75,627.

  • Support: $62,300, where BTC bounced on November 15 and 18, after holding in February, June, July and August. Below that, $57,800, the July low.

  • Resistance: $65,500, a level that turned BTC back in June, July and August. Above that, $74,300.

BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: TradingView

For Bitcoin, the number to watch is the daily ETF flow. A few days of inflows would ease the pressure on $62,300. Another week like this one, with outflows near five times new supply, would make that support much harder to defend.

data.title: Mag 7 Weekly: Nvidia Beat The Street. Leadership Still Owns The Week.
data.description:
This Mag 7 week had one center of gravity. Nvidia (NVDA) reported its first quarter after Jensen Huang stepped down, posted sales that more than doubled, guided above Wall Street, and still closed the week as the clear loser on the board. The market is no longer arguing about whether the chips sell. It is arguing about who runs the company that sells them, and how long customers can keep paying for the buildout.

Through the regular close into Thursday, Nvidia sat near minus 13% for the week and about minus 30% for the month. Alphabet (GOOGL) was the softest of the rest near minus 4%. Amazon (AMZN) was the only name green on the week, helped by the Anthropic IPO story landing right on Mag 7 Thursday. Apple (AAPL) barely moved and still owns the year. Meta Platforms (META), Microsoft (MSFT), and Tesla (TSLA) all finished red without stealing the headline from Nvidia.

Apple remains the Mag 7 year-to-date leader near plus 30% and the only name still hanging near a record. Nvidia is down about 20% for the year and roughly a third off its early-October high. That split is the whole story this week: product cash machines hold; pure AI leadership risk gets marked down hard.

The Scoreboard

Prices and moves as of the latest regular close into Mag 7 Thursday.

Nvidia: The Beat Did Not Buy a Free Pass

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and about $6.7 billion above the Street. Data-center sales were about $107.6 billion, up 110%. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.68 a share versus expectations near $2.47. Fourth-quarter revenue guidance of roughly $127 billion to $133 billion cleared the roughly $125 billion consensus, and management lifted the longer growth frame toward about 75% for the next fiscal year.

None of that stopped the stock from finishing near $151 after a roughly 3% drop on the session after the report. Colette Kress is interim CEO after Huang resigned amid personal-conduct revelations. Board chair Harvey Jones has said Huang will not be rehired, while Huang has said he remains open to returning. Markets hate that open loop when a founder has been the product roadmap, the customer relationships, and the Washington face for three decades.

My take is blunt. The sales machine still works. The leadership machine does not. Analysts can raise earnings estimates and cut price targets in the same breath because the business is strong and the person who built it is gone. Customers still owe Nvidia tens of billions for chips already delivered, which is why the week kept circling one ugly question: can the buyers keep writing those checks if the AI boom slows or if strategy wobbles under a new boss. A beat without a stable captain is just a good quarter with a bad story attached.

Apple Holds the High Ground. Amazon Catches the IPO Day.

Apple (AAPL) closed near $352, still within a couple percent of its recent record and still the Mag 7 year-to-date leader near plus 30%. Market value sits around $5.1 trillion. While Nvidia, Meta, and Alphabet sit far below their highs, Apple keeps looking like the crowded safe seat inside mega-cap tech. That premium can cut both ways. It is also the name least priced as a pure data-center buildout bet, which is exactly why it held up while the AI leadership story cracked.

Amazon (AMZN) was the only Mag 7 stock green on the week, closing near $268 after a late bounce near plus 4% on Wednesday. Thursday is Anthropic IPO day under the ANT ticker after pricing around $83 a share, with reporting putting a fully diluted value near $1.5 trillion. Coverage has Amazon and Alphabet holding large stakes, and Amazon still owns the AWS growth story that keeps it in the Mag 7 conversation even when chip names get hit. Logistics expansion talk into 2027 added a second, quieter support under the stock.

Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, Tesla

Microsoft (MSFT) closed near $508 after a week down about 2.5%. Ignite put Maia 300 and Copilot Workspaces in front of enterprise buyers, with fresh coverage on a longer Azure hardware path with Intel (INTC). The stock still sits below its early-November high because the whole AI complex is being marked on leadership and spend risk.

Meta (META) finished near $616, down about 2% on the week and still roughly 11% lower on the month, with the market still weighing huge AI budgets against free-cash-flow questions and chatter that Meta paused a non-voting share plan. Alphabet (GOOGL) closed near $282 after the softest non-Nvidia Mag 7 week near minus 4% and a month still near minus 17%. Cloud growth is strong in the rearview and the Anthropic stake gives Google a seat at Thursday's IPO, but investors still want proof capex turns into durable profit. Tesla (TSLA) sat near $384, down about 2% on the week, with state-media coverage saying China production keeps climbing. Real factory story. Not enough to outrun a Nvidia succession week.

Bottom Line

This Mag 7 week separated sales from trust. Nvidia proved the AI chip engine can still smash expectations after the founder left. The stock still took the worst week because succession and customer spending power matter more than one guide raise. Apple stayed near a record as the cash-machine leader. Amazon caught the Anthropic IPO day. Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Tesla mostly rode the same AI-risk wave lower. Next week starts with Anthropic trading in public and the same Mag 7 question: who can fund the boom without a leadership hole or a buyer strike.

data.title: Beyond An 81% Revenue Surge: Is Freedom Holding Building A Global Financial Powerhouse?
data.description:
An 81% increase in quarterly revenue would be noteworthy for almost any financial services company. For Freedom Holding Corp. (FRHC), however, the latest results tell a story that extends well beyond a single impressive growth figure.

The international financial services and technology group is undergoing a significant transformation, expanding from its traditional brokerage operations into banking, insurance, payments, telecommunications, and an increasingly broad range of digital services.

On November 16, Freedom Holding announced that revenue for its second fiscal quarter of 2027, ended September 30, 2026, reached $910.1 million, compared with $503.6 million a year earlier.

Net income rose 29% to $46.1 million, while diluted earnings per share increased from $0.58 to $0.76. Total assets climbed to $16.6 billion, up 26% from the end of March.

Those figures suggest a business gaining considerable scale.

Yet beneath the headline growth lies an equally important development: Freedom Holding's traditional brokerage business is no longer its largest source of revenue.

Banking and insurance have moved to the forefront, while the company's investment in a wider digital ecosystem is creating additional growth opportunities and potentially valuable operating efficiencies.

For investors, the central question is whether Freedom Holding can turn this expanding network of businesses into a more profitable, diversified financial enterprise.

The Numbers Behind the Revenue Surge

Freedom Holding's latest quarterly results reveal a dramatic shift in the composition of its business.

Banking revenue nearly tripled, while insurance revenue more than doubled. Together, these two segments accounted for approximately 66% of the company's quarterly revenue.

The breakdown illustrates how significantly the business has evolved.

Source: Freedom Holding Corp., [Form 10-Q] for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

Figure 1. Quarterly revenue by segment (USD millions), compared with the year-earlier quarter. Source: Freedom Holding, September 2026 Form 10-Q.

Banking and insurance generated approximately $363 million of the company's $406 million year-over-year revenue increase.

That means roughly 89% of the additional quarterly revenue came from just two business segments.

Perhaps the most important development is that Freedom Holding is no longer dependent on brokerage as its primary growth engine.

The benefits of that diversification are already becoming apparent. While brokerage revenue declined 5% during the quarter, banking and insurance revenue surged 182% and 133%, respectively, helping drive an 81% increase in consolidated revenue.

This demonstrates one of the fundamental advantages of operating across multiple business lines: weakness in one segment can be offset by strength in others.

Rather than relying on brokerage commissions and trading activity alone, Freedom is developing multiple sources of revenue spanning banking, insurance, investments, payments, and digital services.

That broader foundation could help make the company more resilient to changing market conditions while creating additional opportunities for growth and cross-selling.

Although these businesses are not immune to broader economic risks, their expansion reduces Freedom's reliance on any single revenue stream and strengthens the long-term rationale for its diversified financial-services model.

Banking Emerges as a Major Growth Engine

Banking has become one of Freedom Holding's most important growth drivers.

Quarterly banking revenue reached $298.1 million, compared with $105.7 million a year earlier.

The increase reflects growing lending activities, a larger portfolio of income-generating securities, and gains from securities trading and foreign exchange transactions.

Across the company, interest income rose 53% to $323.9 million.

The expansion is particularly significant because banking provides Freedom Holding with something brokerage alone cannot: a broader relationship with customers' everyday financial activities.

Through Freedom Bank and its digital services, customers can access payments, deposits, loans, investment products, and other financial offerings.

That creates potential opportunities for cross-selling additional services, increasing customer engagement, and generating recurring financial relationships.

As the customer base grows, these interconnected services could become an increasingly valuable source of revenue.

The company's quarterly SEC filing also identifies securities-trading gains and favorable foreign exchange activity among the factors supporting banking revenue.

These can contribute meaningfully to earnings, although they may fluctuate from quarter to quarter.

For investors, the longer-term opportunity lies in the continued expansion of the underlying customer, lending, payment, and service businesses, alongside increasingly consistent profitability.

Insurance Is Becoming Equally Important

Insurance was Freedom Holding's largest revenue segment during the quarter, narrowly exceeding banking.

Revenue increased 133% to $299.2 million, driven substantially by growth in the company's pension annuity insurance operations.

This business serves customers seeking financial protection and longer-term retirement-related products.

The opportunity is meaningful because insurance relationships can extend over many years, potentially strengthening customer retention and providing another source of financial activity within Freedom's ecosystem.

The company reported a 148% increase in net insurance revenue to $254.8 million, supported by growth in new policies and premium inflows.

The expansion also illustrates the advantages of Freedom's broader strategy.

Customers already using its banking or investment services may be interested in insurance products, while insurance customers may eventually explore other financial services offered through the same group.

These complementary relationships could help increase customer engagement and create opportunities for additional revenue.

Of course, insurance growth also brings obligations to policyholders, including future benefit payments and reserve requirements.

The insurance segment generated approximately $9.9 million in net income during the quarter, demonstrating positive profitability even as the business continues expanding.

As the portfolio matures, effective management of underwriting, expenses, and long-term obligations will be important in determining how much of this growing revenue translates into earnings.

The SuperApp Strategy: Bringing Everything Together

Conceptual illustration of Freedom Holding's integrated services strategy.

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of Freedom Holding's business model is its ambition to connect financial and nonfinancial services within a single digital ecosystem.

In Kazakhstan, the company has been developing this approach through its Freedom SuperApp, which brings together banking, investment, insurance, payments, and everyday digital transactions.

The strategy resembles the broader financial-superapp model that has gained traction in several international markets.

Rather than treating banking, brokerage, insurance, and other consumer services as completely separate businesses, Freedom wants customers to use multiple products within an interconnected platform.

The potential advantages are considerable.

A customer who first opens a bank account may later use investment services, obtain insurance, make payments, or purchase other products through the same ecosystem.

That could increase customer engagement and create additional revenue opportunities without requiring the company to acquire an entirely new customer for every service.

Freedom reported approximately 9.27 million customer relationships across its business segments as of September 30, compared with 8.11 million at the end of March.

Banking customers increased from 5.03 million to 5.93 million, while brokerage customers rose from 858,000 to 907,000.

The Other segment, which includes telecommunications, online retail, and digital services, expanded from approximately 1.11 million to 1.55 million customers.

One qualification is important: the company counts customers separately by segment, and individuals using multiple services may appear in more than one category. The 9.27 million total should therefore not be interpreted as 9.27 million unique customers.

Figure 2. Reported customer relationships across business segments; counts may overlap. Source: Freedom Holding, September 2026 Form 10-Q.

Nevertheless, the growth provides evidence that Freedom's expanding platform is attracting substantial activity.

The greater opportunity may lie in encouraging those customers to use multiple services, potentially increasing revenue per customer while reducing the relative cost of acquiring and serving them.

If successful, this could make the overall ecosystem more valuable than its individual businesses operating independently.

Expansion Beyond Kazakhstan

Freedom Holding is also extending its ambitions geographically.

The company reports a presence across 27 countries, and recent acquisitions demonstrate its intention to build a larger international financial-services platform.

One of the most significant developments came on July 31, when Freedom completed the acquisition of approximately 99.3% of Turkish Bank, subsequently renamed Freedom Bank TR.

The acquisition provides the company with an established banking operation in Türkiye, creating a potential foundation for expanding its financial ecosystem into another substantial market.

Rather than starting a banking business entirely from scratch, Freedom gains an existing licensed institution that it can potentially develop using its digital banking experience.

The company has also moved into businesses outside traditional financial services.

In September, it acquired a 60% interest in Bilim Group, an educational technology company operating in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

Other acquisitions during the first half included German chess software developer ChessBase and Estonia-based digital asset services provider Wallet Solutions.

These investments demonstrate the breadth of Freedom's strategy.

Management appears to envision a platform in which financial services, technology, education, entertainment, and consumer transactions reinforce one another.

The potential benefits extend beyond simply adding new revenue streams.

Each additional business may create opportunities to introduce customers to other products, share technology and infrastructure, and develop relationships that extend across multiple services.

International expansion could also gradually reduce dependence on any single geographic market, although Kazakhstan currently remains the company's dominant source of revenue.

Successful integration will be important, particularly when entering industries with different regulatory and operational requirements.

Still, Freedom's growing portfolio of businesses provides multiple avenues for future expansion and creates opportunities that would be difficult to achieve through brokerage operations alone.

Investing in Growth Today, With Potential for Greater Profitability Tomorrow

Freedom Holding's rapid expansion is bringing substantial new revenue, but it is also requiring significant investment.

Total quarterly expenses increased 93% to $859.9 million, outpacing the company's 81% revenue growth.

At first glance, that difference might raise concerns about profitability. However, it is important to consider where the additional spending is going and how those investments could affect future earnings.

Freedom is expanding its banking operations, acquiring businesses, entering new markets, investing in technology, and building infrastructure to support a growing customer base.

Many expanding businesses experience periods when expenses rise ahead of revenue as they establish operations intended to support future growth.

Some of these investments may create longer-term operating advantages. Once technology platforms, distribution networks, and other infrastructure are established, the company may be able to serve additional customers without increasing every category of expense at the same rate.

This creates the potential for economies of scale, where revenue expands faster than the costs required to support it.

Freedom's interconnected ecosystem could provide additional advantages. Customers acquired through one business may use other services, potentially reducing customer-acquisition costs and increasing revenue per customer over time.

Importantly, Freedom is already generating consolidated profits while undertaking this expansion.

Net income increased 29% to $46.1 million during the latest quarter, despite substantial spending across its growing operations.

Figure 3. Revenue and net income both increased year over year. Source: Freedom Holding, second-quarter FY2027 results.

The company's established brokerage business remains particularly profitable, generating approximately $115 million in quarterly net income.

Meanwhile, newer operations within the Other segment, including telecommunications and digital services, reported a net loss of approximately $129 million as Freedom continued investing in their expansion.

Not all those expenses are temporary. Higher interest costs, insurance obligations, employee compensation, and other operating expenses will continue to accompany business growth.

Nevertheless, the central opportunity is clear.

If Freedom can build on its expanding customer base while achieving greater operating efficiency, its growing revenue could eventually translate into stronger profit margins.

The company's next stage of development may therefore be defined not simply by how much its businesses grow, but by how effectively it converts that larger operating scale into earnings.

A Stronger Financial Profile Could Support Expansion

Another encouraging development is growing recognition from credit-rating agencies.

In September, S&P Global Ratings (SPGI) revised the outlook on Freedom Holding and several subsidiaries from stable to positive while affirming their international credit ratings.

Moody's (MCO) also assigned insurance financial strength ratings to two Freedom insurance subsidiaries for the first time.

Freedom Life received a Baa3 rating, placing that subsidiary at the lowest investment-grade level on Moody's scale. Freedom Insurance received a Ba1 rating, one level below investment grade.

These ratings apply to the respective insurance entities and should not be interpreted as investment-grade ratings for Freedom Holding as a whole.

Still, they represent potentially useful developments as the company seeks to strengthen its financial position and expand across additional markets.

Creditworthiness matters particularly for a growing financial institution because access to capital and confidence among counterparties can influence its ability to fund operations and pursue expansion.

Freedom's total assets reached $16.6 billion at the end of September, compared with $13.2 billion six months earlier.

Asset growth demonstrates the increasing scale of the business, although it also needs to be evaluated alongside liabilities, capital adequacy, credit quality, and funding costs.

One outstanding regulatory matter is an ongoing SEC investigation involving certain brokerage settlement practices, accounting, and disclosures. In March 2026, Freedom Holding and CEO Timur Turlov received Wells Notices indicating that SEC staff had preliminarily recommended civil enforcement action. The company and Turlov have challenged that determination, and no formal charges have been publicly announced. The matter remains unresolved, although a Wells Notice does not constitute a finding of wrongdoing.

As Freedom grows, disciplined capital allocation, effective compliance, and operational integration will become increasingly important in supporting its long-term expansion.

What Could Drive the Next Phase of Growth?

Several factors could help determine whether Freedom Holding's current momentum develops into a more durable growth story.

The first is continued expansion in banking and insurance.

Both segments have demonstrated the ability to generate substantial additional revenue. Their continued growth could provide a more diversified earnings base and further reduce reliance on brokerage activity.

The second is the continued development of Freedom's SuperApp and interconnected digital services.

Increasing customer adoption is encouraging, but deeper engagement across multiple products could create additional revenue opportunities and improve operating efficiency.

Third, the Turkish banking acquisition creates a potentially important international opportunity.

Successful integration and growth could demonstrate that Freedom's digital banking model can be extended into additional markets.

Another important factor will be the performance of the company's newer businesses.

The substantial investments currently being made in telecommunications, technology, and other digital services could become more valuable as those operations mature.

If revenue continues expanding while infrastructure and other fixed costs are spread across a growing customer base, these businesses may eventually contribute more meaningfully to consolidated profitability.

Finally, the company has opportunities to strengthen the consistency of its earnings.

Continued growth in lending, customer fees, insurance profitability, and recurring service revenue could complement its more market-sensitive brokerage and trading activities.

Taken together, these developments could make Freedom's business increasingly diversified, efficient, and resilient.

The Bottom Line

Freedom Holding's latest earnings report reveals a company undergoing a significant transformation.

Its 81% quarterly revenue increase is impressive, but the larger story may be the emergence of a diversified financial and technology ecosystem with multiple engines of growth.

Banking and insurance are rapidly expanding, while the company's established brokerage business continues generating substantial profits. Together, these operations provide a broader foundation that could help reduce dependence on any single business and create opportunities across different market conditions.

Freedom's continued investments in technology, infrastructure, and international expansion are also laying the groundwork for potential economies of scale as its newer businesses mature.

Although expenses are growing rapidly and some operations have yet to achieve profitability, the company is already generating higher consolidated earnings while expanding its reach.

If Freedom Holding can successfully integrate its growing businesses, deepen relationships with its customers, and capitalize on the efficiencies of its expanding ecosystem, it could emerge as an increasingly significant force in international financial services.

The company's remarkable revenue growth is already evident. The next chapter could be even more interesting: turning that expanding financial ecosystem into a powerful engine for sustained profitability and long-term value creation.
